Mr. Speaker, I do not know what that point of order was in aid of.
As I was saying last Monday, I wish the Parliamentary Secretary would have stood up and said on each of the amendments which we have debated why they were not acceptable to the Government and for what reasons. Following the discussions in the committee on each of these items, my colleague, the Liberal Party critic and myself came in with amendments going at the same matters in a different way, hoping that that would satisfy the Government's earlier objections. We still cannot find out why they do not like these amendments. The Parliamentary Secretary did not rise. I noticed that the chairman of the committee was here for prayers, but he has now left. I was hoping that he would rise.
I do not think an employer should be allowed to take a statement from an employee involved in an occurrence, incident or accident until after the investigator for the board has taken a statement. In other words, just like the scene of an occurrence or accident being quarantined until the board investigator has arrived at the scene, so should those employees who are affected. They should be quarantined from the tender mercies of their employer who might want to take a statement for disciplinary purposes or other reasons. That is why I feel the Hon. Member's amendment does not go far enough. However, it is a good amendment in that it protects the confidentiality of the statement taken from the employee. This is a good principle and one that we support. I urge government Members to accept it as well.
There is not sufficient protection either in the collective agreement as it would pertain to this Bill or in other statutes, and we want to secure the privilege of those statements given by employees, be they management or rank and file. I urge government Members to accept this amendment. It will be supported by my colleagues and I, and I trust that the Government has seen the error of its earlier ways and will accept this amendment.

Motion No. 10
That Bill C-2 be amended in Clause 24 by adding immediately
after line 36 at page 22 the following:
"(3) The Board shall append to the final report any recommendations made in the draft report but not included in the public report, and recommendations and comments made by the Minister of Transport or any other Minister or observer designated as such under 23(2)(d)."
He said: Mr. Speaker, in the committee, we initially tried to have three parts of Clause 24 deleted from the Bill because of something to which all members of the committee agreed. The Canadian Transportation Accident Investigation and Safety Board must not only be independent but must be seen to be independent. Lo and behold, the Bill provides for a draft of the final report of the board on any accident or incident in any one of four modes of transportation to be sent to the Minister and other observers to make comments and representations.
We lost out on getting that provision deleted from the Bill so the purpose of this amendment is to ensure that not only is no influence attempted but that there is no
perception that some influence may be attempted to be placed on the board by some external force and go unnoticed.
If a major change is made to the final report, the public one, the only way of finding that out is to compare it to the draft report which quite correctly has limited release. Originally, we wanted to do away with the concept of a draft report altogether. Then we tried to see that the draft report have wider distribution. This failed because of the very good reason of confidentiality. That position may not be supported by the Liberals, though I hope they will support it, or Members on the Government side. Government Members certainly do not want to see this happen. However, it was suggested by several groups that we must make this attempt.
The Chief Executive Officer of the Canadian Railway Labour Association representing some nine railway unions said that the unions wanted no part of this, would not be the slightest bit interested in getting a draft report and that the draft of the final report should not go out to anyone.
During the course of an investigation and during the course of board hearings, the Minister will have an observer on hand as well as at the site of the accident or incident. So will the other representatives of employees or companies involved. Those who qualify as observers under the legislation will have ample opportunity to make representations both to the chief investigator and to the board when it is deliberating, hearing witnesses and receiving evidence obtained by the investigator and provided by other sources. There will be ample opportunity for them to make their views known and to comment on whether or not they think there are any omissions or if an investigation was carried on improperly or insufficiently before the final report is drafted. Therefore, I do not see any need for a draft of the final report to be sent out for people to make comments on.
Since people will be allowed to make comments on a draft report, we are trying to provide here that any representations, comments or requests made by the Minister or any other Minister or any qualified observer who receives the draft of the final report shall be appended to the final report. Then we can check to see what differences there are between the draft report and the final report. It will all be out in the open as to what
June 16, 1989

kind of comments and recommendations were made by the Minister or others.
I do not want anyone in the Chamber to get mixed up. There are interim reports which have nothing to do with this section. Interim reports are covered in Clause 25, and will be made by the board as and when it deems necessary to correct something that occurred and could be a cause of further accident or occurrences. This will have the matter corrected without waiting for a final report. The Minister may request interim reports if he thinks there is something wrong somewhere and wants to be able to act on it. He can call the board up and request an interim report. We are not suggesting that there be any changes in that.
However, I do not think the draft of the final report should go out to anyone anyway, but since it is going to, the public has a right to know. It should be perceived as well as believed that the board is independent; that no improper pressure or influence was attempted on the board in order to get it to change the draft of the final report.
That is why we are asking in this amendment that all representations made by the Minister or other observers have to be appended to the final report. Then everyone will know, and that will enhance the independence of the board. It will not only appear to be independent but it will be. All its proceedings will be in public, unless for a specific reason it orders some portion of a hearing to be in camera, but generally speaking everything is out in the open.
That is why in this draft report there should be no opportunity or temptation for anyone to attempt, in an improper manner to influence the board or get it to change what it feels should be in the final report. If the board does make a change, we can see what requests or representations were made, what change the board made, and the reasons for it. If they are proper and justified, that is fine. Again, it is out in the open.
The Government should be leading the line-up to enlarge and enhance the real independence of the board. This amendment does in fact do that. I hope the Government will decide that at least this amendment does improve the legislation, does enhance the independence of the board and ensures even more that no one
Accident Investigation
can exercise any undue influence, pressure or improper action upon the board, its members or any of its staff.
Once the final report is delivered to the President of the Privy Council, copies should go to all the Ministries and to interested observers and interested parties. I presume that the report will also be referred to the Standing Committee on Transport. If it is felt that anything is fundamentally wrong in the report, by the Minister or any of the observers, the Minister can make further inquiries. If there are omissions or inadequacies in the final report, it can be gone into again by the Minister or by anyone else he may appoint to do that.
I hope the amendment will find favour with all my colleagues and that it will receive the support of the Government and the Official Opposition.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Regina-Lumsden (Mr. Benjamin) spoke with such characteristic eloquence on the rationale and with powerful reasoning and persuasion behind the authorship of the amendment that he proposes to the House that there is not much that I or any other Member could possibly add that would enlighten Members.
We in the Official Opposition support the amendment of the Hon. Member. We support the basic notion that justice must not only be done, but must be seen to be done, and the independence of the board must not only be practised, but must be seen to be practised.
What the Member is proposing in his amendment is that, given in the process of investigating and coming to conclusions about an accident or occurrence in the transportation field, and quite possibly a loss of life, it is extremely important that public confidence in our investigation agency be maintained, especially in the light of the Gander experience and the deep division on the CASB board, the conflicting opinions about what caused the crash and terrible loss of life in Gander.
Given that it is important that public confidence be maintained, the Member proposes to the House that any draft report, and there is a provision for a draft report in this Bill, submitted to Ministers of the Crown prior to a public release of a final report, and any draft report cany with it an obligation that any comments by Ministers, and more importantly any subsequent changes to the draft that are reflected in the final report, be noted when the final report is released. The public will then have an opportunity to see whether between the draft and the release of the final report there have been any changes, and if there have been, who recommended them and on
June 16, 1989

Accident Investigation
whose advice were changes made. In other words, the public needs to know there is not an ability behind closed doors or in secret away from the public's eye to change a recommendation.
I hope that the people appointed by the Government to serve on this board are people of such credibility and integrity that that type of practice would not be permitted in any case. I would hope that the Ministers of the Crown undertake their responsibilities in such a manner that they would not attempt to exercise that type of influence in any case. I and all Members would expect that.
However, if there is nothing to hide, and I submit there is nothing to hide and we take the Government at face value in submitting this Bill, then there should be no hesitation in supporting the amendment of the Hon. Member and providing for the full disclosure of recommendations made at the draft stage, and more importantly the ability to see what changes were brought about in the final report as a result of those recommendations made at the draft stage.
We support the amendment of the Hon. Member for Regina-Lumsden.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte) moved:
subtopic: CANADIAN TRANSPORTATION ACCIDENT INVESTIGATION AND SAFETY BOARD ACT
speechtext:
Motion No. 11
That Bill C-2 be amended in Clause 32 by striking out lines 19 to
25 at page 31.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the final amendment proposed by the Liberal Party to Bill C-2, but frankly I think it goes far beyond the purview of the Bill, which is the whole question of accident investigation. I submit that the amendment is fundamental to Members of the House because the principle expressed in Clause 32 has a direct impact on the whole notion of the principle of fundamental justice.
Members of Parliament who have not been part of the committee process should know that the clause we are seeking to amend by this motion is Clause 32 of the Bill. It is a clause that sets out the responsibilities of an investigator, that is somebody who goes out and conducts the investigation into an accident on behalf of the multi-modal agency.
This particular clause sets out the responsibilities of an investigator vis-a-vis a court of law, in particular whether or not there is litigation before a court of law having to do with the cause of an accident when victims or their families may be attempting to seek legal redress. In short, they are suing those who may have been responsible for an accident.
I want to read the clause that I am trying to amend, because I think Members will understand that what we are talking about is far more important that just this Bill. There are three sections to Clause 32. The section I am attempting to amend reads:
An investigator whose evidence may be admitted by affidavit under this section is not compellable to appear as a witness in the proceedings unless the court, coroner or other person or body before whom the proceedings are conducted so orders, for special cause.
I ask Members to reflect upon that. The evidence of an investigator may be admitted before a court of law, yet the investigator who submitted and drafted the affidavit is himself not automatically compelled to appear in a
June 16, 1989

court of law to defend the conclusions he has reached. The defence does not have an automatic right to crossexamine the author of an affidavit that is submitted in a court of law as evidence. I want Members to think about, especially those who are members of the Bar, what this amendment says.
As I just said, this clause is comprised of three sections. In referring to the affidavit, the first section of the clause reads:
-in any legal, disciplinary or other proceedings and, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, is proof of the truth of those observations.
In the absence of proof to the contrary and in the absence of evidence to the contrary, the affidavit as submitted by the investigator will be accepted as proof of the truth of those observations.
We have a situation in which an affidavit authored by an investigator may be submitted to a court of law. In the absence of evidence to the contrary, it will be accepted as proof of the truth of the observations. The investigator himself has no automatic obligation to appear before a court of law to defend his observations, unless the party in question who takes exception to those observations proves to a judge that there is cause to disturb the investigator in his normal duties and compel him to appear before a court.
The fundamental principle of justice, I submit, is the right to cross-examination. It is an automatic right. I question that notwithstanding putting this clause in the Bill whether or not any judge will pay any attention to it anyway. I submit it is not for Parliament to make any kind of determination on who should or should not appear before a court of law, to make any kind of judgment or to try to send any kind of signal to a coroner or a judge that only in exceptional circumstances should an investigator of the Crown be called to defend his observations. I submit Parliament in this context really has no role whatsoever in trying to give direction to a court, to a coroner, or to an inquirer.
The effect of my amendment is simply to wipe out entirely subclause 32(3) which indicates:
An investigator whose evidence may be admitted by affidavit under this section is not compellable to appear as a witness in the proceedings unless the court, coroner or any other person or body-so orders, for special cause.
Accident Investigation
Its seems to me it is not for Parliament to make that determination. It is for a court. I do not think that Parliament in any way, shape, or form should seek to give advice to a court or should seek to indicate that it is our desire, unless there is special cause, that the normal right of the defence should not be exercised.
I submit that if we care or value at all the fundamental notion of justice, which must have as its centre-piece the right of cross-examination, Parliament would be acting in a wise and judicious manner in simply removing a clause that not only directly impacts on the ability of people to cross-examine a witness in terms of the proceedings of the multi-modal Accident Investigation Board but sets a rather onerous and dangerous precedent in legislation enacted by Parliament.
I cannot find anywhere in any federal legislation any precedent for this kind of clause being contained in the Bill. It does not exist in any other legislation that has ever been passed or contemplated by the Parliament of Canada.
By the way, I submit that the Government means no harm; there is no devious plot nor evil design on the part of the Government. It happens to be one of those things that in the process of drafting a Bill is slipped in, perhaps with another intention.
I can tell Members that the intention is that investigators are quite frequently tied up in court having to defend their observations as contained in affidavits. The Government is concerned that their investigators spend their time out investigating accidents, not being tied up in courts. That is a fair comment on the part of the Government, but which is the greater need? Is it the need to free up our investigators from a court of law, or the absolute primary requirement to ensure that justice is upheld and that the fundamental right of cross-examination is maintained?
It may be inconvenient for the Government to have investigators tied up in the courts. It may be inconvenient for the investigators. It may tie up valuable time, but we cannot solve a problem of inconvenience on the part of investigators by tinkering with one of the fundamental tenets of our justice system, the right to cross-examination.
I do not allege any evil design. I do not allege any plot or conspiracy. I simply allege sloppy drafting of this Bill. I simply allege that those who seek to solve the problem of an investigator spending more time than he likes in a

Accident Investigation
court of law have interfered in a fundamental way in sound and basic principles of justice. I would call upon Members to remove this clause.
The only effect of removing this clause will be to put back into the hands of the courts, the coroner, and the judges, back where it belongs in the judicial system or normal body of inquiry, the decision on who appears or does not appear as a witness.
Parliament should not be attempting to give any direction whatsoever. We should not deny or reduce even in the slightest manner the possibility of a lawyer, representing a client, having an investigator come to defend the accuracy of his observations.
I hope that Parliament, in a non-partisan way and in the interests of producing a better Bill and a good Bill, will accept the amendment that I propose. I submit this simply in the interest of ensuring that we produce good legislation and do not inadvertently interfere, in a Draconian way, in the proper proceedings of justice.

Mr. Speaker, I must confess that I am something of two minds on this amendment. The clause that my good friend wishes to have deleted ends with the words:
- unless the court, coroner or other person or body before whom the proceedings are conducted so orders-

speechtext: "For special cause". Leave it to the court.

subtopic: CANADIAN TRANSPORTATION ACCIDENT INVESTIGATION AND SAFETY BOARD ACT
speechtext:
Of course, that is designed, I gather, so that when there is a lawsuit involving hundreds of millions of dollars following an air crash which drags on for three or four years, a top-notch investigator of the board is not spending months and months sitting around in the court room. That is nice. I agree that it is not a good thing to have happen.
On the other side of the coin, the remarks of my colleague are well taken. If an attorney for a claimant wishes to dispute evidence in an affidavit or brings in other expert witnesses who dispute what is in an affidavit of an investigator, all that attorney has to do is ask the court or the coroner to order that he appear. However, that does not guarantee that the court or the coroner will so order. If the court decides not to issue an order, there
is no way the author of the affidavit can be questioned as to its accuracy or otherwise.
The deletion of this clause means that an attorney in a court, or one involved in litigation following an accident, may just call him as a witness. If he does not come, then he can ask for a subpoena. However, it makes it easier for an attorney who, let us say, is acting for the families of people who were killed in an occurrence. Deleting this clause makes it easier for that attorney to have the investigator appear.

subtopic: CANADIAN TRANSPORTATION ACCIDENT INVESTIGATION AND SAFETY BOARD ACT
speechtext: It maintains the status quo. That is what it does.

subtopic: CANADIAN TRANSPORTATION ACCIDENT INVESTIGATION AND SAFETY BOARD ACT
speechtext:
In other words it keeps things the way they are. Frankly, if a court were not to order it, I suspect there would be appeals and a higher court would strike this clause down. I think it would be thrown out of court.
I think that the Parliamentary Secretary would have to agree with me, even though I am not a lawyer and I do not think he is either.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: CANADIAN TRANSPORTATION ACCIDENT INVESTIGATION AND SAFETY BOARD ACT
speechtext: Thank goodness.

subtopic: CANADIAN TRANSPORTATION ACCIDENT INVESTIGATION AND SAFETY BOARD ACT
speechtext:
From many a legal discussion I have had with legal eagles, they think that this is a pretty weak piece of legislation, a pretty weak clause which is not likely to stand up on appeal, and that a higher court will just strike it down. That would involve appeal after appeal and dragging the case out even longer at great cost to everyone concerned, including the Government.
On balance, I agree with the Hon. Member. I think that his motion should be accepted. We should delete subclause 32(3). I do not think it serves much of a purpose anyway. It will not accomplish what the Government would like it to accomplish.
I fully agree with my colleague that anything that even appears to impinge upon what is a fundamental tenet of our justice system is not good law. We should not have anything in the Bill which appears to impinge. It might be all very well to say: "Well, this would never happen anyway, the court would order him to appear, or the coroner would order him to appear". We cannot be sure of that. In that situation in a court case subsequent to an accident justice would not be fully done. If a court or coroner fails to issue an order then justice would not be fully done.
I agree with my colleague that this is not a partisan issue. I think all members of the committee felt strongly about this legislation and think that it is basically good
June 16, 1989

legislation. We have moved some amendments and a few of them were accepted at committee. We did this to try to make a better Bill. That was the intention of all members from all sides in the committee. It was the intent of the motions my colleagues and I have moved at report stage. They are in order to make a better Bill.
I sometimes wonder why I spend so much time trying to help rewrite the Government's legislation in order to make it better. Maybe we should just let it go through as it is and let the Government get into a lot of trouble. However, if one is a responsible parliamentarian, one tries to do one's job and hopes to get the Government to mend its ways.
I do not think there is any malicious intent or devious intent on the part of the Government. It was just an attempt to set some kind of a limit on how much time an investigator might have to spend in a trial because he is required as a witness. I do not think this clause will accomplish that. The greatest danger is that the right to cross-examine is harmed in any way, shape, or form. I hope the Government will accept this amendment as well as the others which we have put forward when it comes to voting on them on Monday night.

speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, May 26, consideration of the motion of Mrs. Landry that Bill C-10, an Act relating to the forgiveness of debts incurred or assumed in respect of certain official development assistance loans made by the Government of Canada to the Governments of certain countries in sub-Saharan Africa, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: FORGIVENESS OF DEBTS (SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should emphasize that this Bill has the support of our Party and I hope the support of all Members of the House.
Before we vote on the Bill I want to take this opportunity to discuss, for a few moments at least, the issues which underlie this legislation.
The Bill itself would forgive the debts of certain sub-Saharan African countries. As I understand it, the House has already provided in past budgets for the funds that would be covered by this Bill, but the Act itself is necessary. It gives us an opportunity to speak directly to the issue of Third World debt and to speak, therefore, about one of the most pressing problems in the world, that of the crushing burden of debt on societies which comprise probably two-thirds of the people of the planet.
If we were to pause and review our stewardship of this planet, we would quickly come to see four related problems: first, the problem of the environment; second,

June 16, 1989

the arms race; third, the issue of lack of freedom; and fourth, the issue of poverty. As the Brundtland report has so eloquently and clearly shown, these issues are inextricably linked.
Today in this country the issue of the environment stands at the forefront. The environment is threatened, not just by this society's overuse of resources, but by the tremendous increase in the use of chemicals and other substances which attack the air we breathe, the ozone layer, the oceans, and the waters. Throughout the world the environment is under attack, in part because of the extraordinary expenditure on the arms race and because of the distortion of economic resources that go to the arms race. This in turn has put pressure on Governments and others to seek to control in the most arbitrary ways the freedom of their people who seek themselves to press for the use of resources for the basic fundamentals of human existence.
All this has driven millions, if not billions, of people in the world to live in crushing poverty, which in turn puts pressure on the environment and resources. In many countries of the world, the forests, the waters, and the lands are under assault because of the desperate need of people just to meet the basics.
With regard to our responsibility as a country, most of us live in an affluence that previously was undreamed of in human history. Our affluence assaults the environment of the Third World and contributes to the poverty of so much of the Third World. Since the end of the Second World War, Canada has participated in efforts to try to improve the economies and the social conditions in other parts of the world. One of the major ways that has been accomplished has been through Official Development Assistance. For years, however, our Official Development Assistance has been in the form of loans to Third World countries, which have normally required repayment over a period of time.
At the same time, we have been giving a relatively paltry sum to assist the development. We have been making it increasingly impossible for Third World countries to meet the obligations we have imposed upon them. Changes in exchange rates, lack of fixed prices for commodities, and total instability in the international economy imposed through our multinational institutions have created a situation in which Third World countries have found it impossible or very difficult to meet the obligations imposed on them. Probably more money is
leaving, both from government and commercial loans, to pay them back and to pay the interest thereon than we are turning back to the Third World to assist it in its economic development.
There have been a number of major studies in this regard. The Brandt report highlighted a number of years ago north-south issues, our interdependence as a planet, and the need to deal with Third World debt for our own interest economically.
The recent document entitled Our Common Future, commonly known as the Brundtland report, named after the chair of that committee, has linked those problems with the environment. This Bill would confirm at least the minimum, that is, the forgiving of debts we imposed on the Third World. The repayment of them has made it even more difficult for that cycle to be broken.
I would like to use this opportunity to call the Government to account for another policy which has been imposed, that is, the reduction in the budget of Official Development Assistance. It seems to me that it is the height of hypocrisy for this Government, on the one hand, to bring forward Bill C-10 forgiving debts which in some sense have already been forgiven and, on the other hand, to reduce significantly the funds provided through Official Development Assistance to break the cycle of poverty in the Third World.
I had an opportunity many years ago, in 1972-1973, to spend a year in Tanzania on a CIDA project. One of the feelings I had at that time was that while this program was on the face of it a donation by Canada to Tanzania and to the Third World, in the final analysis, myself and my family gleaned much more from Tanzania than Tanzania got from the program, even though I hope I was able to provide some assistance in the work that I did. Hundreds of thousands of Canadians have worked in the Third World under various programs: CIDA, CUSO, Canada World Youth, OXFAM, and many others. We have learned as much from these as we have given.
The Third World has given much to this country in the way of its resources, in its understanding of human history, and in both beauty and other values. The very least we can do is to adopt this Bill, and from this Bill we must take other more important steps toward the alleviation of poverty in the Third World. We must restore the cuts to Official Development Assistance. We must use our role in the IMF and the World Bank to assist the total restructuring of the international economy so that
June 16, 1989

this critical problem that faces the world today can be truly addressed in the immediate years ahead.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the recent crisis in China, my office in Scarborough was contacted by a constituent who was unable to reach his son.
Bill Brown's son, Stephen, was teaching at the University of China in Wuhan. Officials at External Affairs worked tirelessly to locate him. This morning Stephen Brown arrived safely in Hong Kong.
On behalf of Mr. Brown and his family, I want to thank the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and his officials for the outstanding assistance that they provided. Their work throughout this crisis has been exemplary and I applaud those efforts.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the events of National Environment Week which did not receive as much public attention as it deserved was
the announcement of Environment Canada's decision to honour hundreds of volunteer weather observers across the country.
These observers record morning and evening temperatures and the total precipitation each day in their respective areas. The data is forwarded to the Atmospheric Environment Service on a monthly basis and entered into the National Climatological Archives.
Since 1871 a network of 176 volunteer observers has now grown to approximately 2,300 strong. Climatological awards for volunteer service have been issued in my constituency of Brandon-Souris to the staff members at the International Peace Gardens, the Spence family of Medora, the Sexton family of Deloraine and the Lowe family of Waskada.
In addition a special award to the Renton family of Deloraine has been granted for 24 years of high quality weather reporting.
Thanks to these and hundreds of other volunteers, Canada's Climatological Archives have been greatly enriched.

subtopic: PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC OF CHINA-OPPOSITION TO EXECUTION OF DEMONSTRATORS
PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC OF CHINA-OPPOSITION TO EXECUTION OF DEMONSTRATORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government of the People's Republic of China continues with the total and absolute repression of its people. The Chinese Government has arrested and imprisoned individuals who had the courage to tell the whole world, via the electronic media, the truth about the tragic events in China.

Canadians are particularly concerned with the death sentences imposed on three reformers in Shanghai. These protesters were accused of burning a train which minutes before smashed through a human barricade killing six demonstrators.
Reports say that no one was injured or killed as a result of the blaze set on the train. In my opinion, the real criminals were the authorities who ordered the train to proceed. Now, Mr. Speaker, the death toll as a result of this incident will increase to nine, unless people in

June 16, 1989
Canada write to the Chinese Embassy urging them not to impose the death penalty.
I call on the Government and all Canadians to express their deepest condemnation on the imminent execution of Chinese demonstrators. The global community must do everything in its power to prevent China's descent in ever deeper political turmoil.

Mr. Speaker, this weekend representatives of the Canada Safety Council are meeting in Winnipeg with seniors' interest groups to begin preparations for National Seniors Safety Week, November 12 to November 18.
The theme of the event is "Safeguard the Best Years of Your Life". Its purpose is to draw attention to safety issues affecting seniors, to identify accidents and health hazards which can confront seniors in the home and to promote measures which can be taken to reduce deaths.
Older Canadians sustain a rate of accidental death and injury approximately three times higher than the rest of the population. More than 20 per cent of deaths are caused by home injury with accidents due to falls heading the list.
A conference such as this one is vitally important in improving the quality of life of Canadian seniors. I applaud the council for its initiative in organizing this event and extend my best wishes for a successful National Seniors Safety Week.

Mr. Speaker, recently as part of the National Access Awareness Week, the Secretary of State (Mr. Weiner) presented the first ever five star community awards at the annual conference of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities in Vancouver.
The awards recognize communities across the country that demonstrate a strong commitment to the ideal of
full and equal access for disabled Canadians in the five star areas of transportation, housing, employment, recreation and education.
The awards ceremony was the crowning moment for a very successful National Access Awareness Week in which more than 400 communities participated.
The Minister gave 16 awards to the civic leaders of 14 cities, towns, districts and a regional municipality in recognition of their action to improve community access for people with disabilities. Two cities, Kitchener and Ottawa, each received two awards.
Let us join all Canadians in congratulating this year's recipients of five star community awards for their contribution to the integration of people with disabilities into the mainstream of Canadian society.

Mr. Speaker, last night at a company work site on Plinkquet Street in my riding of St. Boniface thousands of litres of petroleum products exploded, shooting clouds of smoke, and I quote from the newspaper report:
-hundreds of metres into the air, creating an inferno of flame too hot for firefighters to approach-
Between 150 and 200 homes were evacuated within two kilometres of the fire. At least six chemicals were stored at the plant. One, in particular, methylene chloride, becomes an extremely toxic hydrochloric acid when exposed to air and mixed with moisture in the lungs.
I call upon the Minister of National Defence (Mr. McKnight) to provide this House with details of his Department's involvement, if any, in the evacuation and subsequent handling of this particular situation. I also call upon the Minister to inform this House as to how well the evacuation procedures undertaken last night worked.
I would call upon the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Beatty) and the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) to inform the House regarding the potential health hazards which may have occurred and which still may be of concern to the residents of St. Boniface and the surrounding areas.
June 16, 1989

maintopic: RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE CANMET PROJECT JOINT ACTION COMMITTEE
RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE CANMET PROJECT JOINT ACTION COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canmet project joint action committee in northwestern Quebec submitted its report on June 12, 1989 to (Quebec) Mines Minister Raymond Savoie and to Assistant Deputy Minister Marc Denis Everell, who is responsible for Canmet. At a press conference, Claude Drouin, committee chairman and executive director of the Quebec Mining Association, reviewed the contents of the report and the committee's recommendations.
The committee's mandate was to support the emergence of a centre of excellence for mineral technology in northwestern Quebec. Public consultations made the committee members aware of 13 interesting site combinations in the area of Rouyn-Noranda and Val-d'Or. The committee unanimously chose the Or Val site, which belongs to Aurizon Mines in the Val-d'Or mining area located in Abitibi-Temiscamingue. Mr. Speaker, this is an excellent choice because this site is ideal for establishing Canmet's mineral technology research laboratory in Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today on behalf of the New Democratic Party to express our concern about the continued persecution of Ahmadi Muslims in Pakistan.
In Pakistan there are approximately five million followers of the Ahmadiyya movement in Islam. The Ahmadi Muslims are peace-loving people celebrating their one-hundredth centenary this year. Sadly, the Pakistan Government has prohibited centenary celebrations at the international headquarters at Rabwah. This
repressive action is consistent with government behaviour towards the Ahmadiyya movement.
Ahmadi publications are censored, their right to freedom of assembly is violated and government measures incite intolerance toward them. Discrimination is a daily fact of life.
Actions against the Ahmadi people extend to violence. Ahmadiyya Mosques are regularly vandalized. Such an incident occurred as recently as last week. In April of this year a large mob set on fire over 50 homes. Many Ahmadi have been assaulted and some have been killed.
It was hoped that this persecution would end with the coming to power of Benazir Bhutto but this has not been the case.
I urge the Canadian Government to express in the strongest terms to the Pakistan Government that the actions against the Ahmadi people are unacceptable. I have already written to the Pakistan ambassador on behalf of the NDP.

Mr. Speaker, today the arts world, and especially the Royal Winnipeg Ballet, is in mourning. At a press conference held in Winnipeg last night, the Ballet's artistic co-ordinator announced that their principal dancer, Mr. David Peregrine, 34 years old, tragically lost his life in a plane crash in Alaska.
Mr. Speaker, we all know that some day we will have to leave this earth, but we are rarely given prior notice. And when death takes away someone in the full flower of his professional life, the shock is even more intense.
On behalf of my fellow Members, I would like to extend our sincerest condolences to Mr. Peregrine's family and also to his family in the arts, the Royal Winnipeg Ballet, one of Canada's most prestigious ballet groups.

June 16, 1989

subtopic: TAGWI SECONDARY SCHOOL "REACH FOR THE TOP" TEAM
TAGWI SECONDARY SCHOOL "REACH FOR THE TOP" TEAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the people of Stormont-Dundas, I would like to congratulate Ihgwi secondary school of Avonmore, Ontario, on the victory of their Reach for the Top team at the national championships which were recently held in Winnipeg.
The Thgwi Team, comprised of coach Dan Maloney and students Allan Coleman, Stuart Pollock, Peter Simard, Claude Theoret and Neil Wheeler, can be proud of the excellent manner in which they represented their school and their province. They are indeed worthy champions.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday and today, we read in the newspapers that both Opposition parties are going to resort to a fundraising method that is, quite frankly, outrageous. With the help of their friends in the financial world, our friends in the NDP and the Liberal Party are not only going to finance their operations by using credit cards, they also intend to swell their ranks by urging Canadians to borrow, at a time when a parliamentary committee is debating the skyrocketing interest charges on credit card balances, and even Opposition Members are criticizing banking practices on behalf of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, the precarious financial circumstances of these two Parties seem to be more important than the interests of consumers. Personally, I feel Canadians will soon realize whose side the Opposition is on.
Voters did not put their trust in them on November 21 last year, and history now proves they were right. The Liberals, the world's experts on debt, have now embarked on a new era, an era of double talk. Our NDP friends, those sworn enemies of the Establishment, have just made a major about-face.
Mr. Speaker, the two Oppositions Parties are absolutely shameless!

Mr. Speaker, 1992 will be the fiftieth anniversary of the Alaska Highway. We, in the Yukon and northern B.C., are inviting the world to celebrate this anniversary with us by coming north and driving the highway.
In fact, the federal Department of Public Works has recently published a brochure on the highway which promotes this event. One activity will be a car rally.
It is crucial that the necessary funds are allocated to highway maintenance now to ensure that travelling this route is a pleasant experience, not only for northerners but for our visitors from all over the world and for the exciting activities planned.
For two years, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. MacKay) has received hundreds of signatures on petitions. There have been unanimous all-Party resolutions from the Yukon Legislature.
There have been numerous interventions by myself asking this Government to recognize the importance of this sole land route to northern B.C. and the Yukon.
I call upon the Government to immediately increase the level of funding for maintenance and improvement of the highway. Let's do Canada proud in 1992.

speakeroldname: Mr. Patrick Boyer (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today 300 African elephants will be slaughtered by poachers and their tusks cut away by chain-saws to supply big bucks for the international illegal ivory trade.
Yesterday, 300 elephants were killed, tomorrow, there will be another 300. Altogether this year some 70,000 African elephants will be slaughtered.
June 16, 1989

Yesterday the Government of Canada announced that this fall it will vote to move the African elephant to the highest level of protection, that which is currently enjoyed by the Asian elephant under the convention for the protection of endangered species. In the meantime, the Government has indicated it will impose new restrictions to ensure that Canada does not become a dumping ground as part of the illicit ivory traffic. It is actions like that which Canada has taken and must continue to take as part of a global response to see that the endangered species on this planet get the protection they deserve.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on two matters today. First, I note with sorrow that the Royal Winnipeg Ballet has been hit by tragedy again in the death of its principal dancer, David Peregrine.
Mr. Peregrine received international recognition when he won the Bronze Medal at the World Ballet Concour, partnered with Evelyn Hart. He had been with the Ballet since 1975 and its principal dancer since 1980. Mr. Peregrine will be greatly missed by the company.

Mr. Speaker, Consolidated Professor Mines Ltd. has recently applied to operate a gold mine at Shoal Lake, Ontario, the source of Winnipeg's drinking water. A recurring consequence of the mining of gold is the production of arsenic. As a result, there is a fear that Winnipeg's water could become contaminated.
The building of the mine would touch on several areas of federal responsibility, namely fisheries, Indian Affairs, interprovincial waterways and international affairs since Shoal Lake is an arm of Lake of the Woods, an international waterway.
Further, this Government has already promised Canadians a safe drinking water act. This is the perfect opportunity for the Government to demonstrate in
Oral Questions
action, not just words, its commitment to the environment.
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) has pledged to Canadians that he would put the environment ahead of profits. Let the Minister demonstrate this commitment today by putting the safety of over half a million peoples drinking water ahead of the profits of one company.
I urge the Government to listen to the Winnipeg Water Protection group and undertake a full federal environmental impact assessment.

subsubtopic: VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS IN PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC OF CHINA-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
The Minister met with the Ambassador of the People's Republic of China yesterday, I think. Did he have the opportunity to express to him the indignation Canadians feel with the ever more frightening increase in the number of violations of the most basic human rights in China, and in particular, did he warn the Ambassador that the killing or execution of students who were sentenced in such summary fashion could have very harmful consequences for future relations between the Government of Canada and his country?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS IN PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC OF CHINA-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had a meeting here yesterday with the Ambassador of the People's Republic of China. I expressed the grave concern of the Government of Canada and Canadians with respect to reports on the treatment and execution of students in China.
I indicated that it would be impossible for Canada to consider a "business as usual" situation, as suggested by some Chinese spokespersons. I stressed the importance of this issue for all Members of the House.
In fact, I gave the Ambassador a copy of the official report of last week's Debates to show clearly and directly what was discussed and the questions and answers here

June 16, 1989
Oral Questions
in the House, so as to leave no doubt in the Chinese leaders' minds as to what Canadians think.
I asked that our opinions be passed on to China's leaders.

subtopic: ACTIONS TO BE TAKEN AT UNITED NATIONS
ACTIONS TO BE TAKEN AT UNITED NATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Minister for his words. Certainly, it will be more significant than just words if Canada takes some initiative at the Security Council at the United Nations. I understand that the Minister is still looking at this possibility.
Ambassador Fruitier will be here next week. Will he then be in a position to tell us precisely what type of specific actions Canada could take at the UN to enhance the positions which the Minister is indicating by words but not yet by action should be taken.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ACTIONS TO BE TAKEN AT UNITED NATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in so far as actions are concerned, the Hon. Member and the House will know that Canada has recalled our ambassador for consultation, as other countries, I believe, have not yet done. We are actively examining actions that can be taken through the United Nations.
I am asked a specific question as to whether or not Ambassador Fortier will be in a position next week to indicate precisely what action might be taken. I cannot answer that question. I do not know whether he will be in a position next week.
I can assure the Hon. Member that we are examining every avenue that is open to us which would result in effective action. Next Thursday morning I will be convening, at the Prime Minister's request, a national round table involving Canadians expert in China, including Canadians of Chinese origin, so that we can supplement the work of the Government at home and internationally with the advice of the Canadians who are knowledgeable about China.
I do not think there is any doubt about the attitude of the Government or the people of Canada. There is, given the nature of international institutions, the challenge in trying to find ways to make our views be felt effectively. I assure the House that we are pursuing that vigorously.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary. Can the Minister confirm this morning that there have been a number of defections from the Chinese embassy here in Ottawa and that a number of Chinese have asked to remain in Canada? If so, could the Minister tell the House that these people are welcome and that everything will be done to make it possible for them to remain in Canada and obtain landed immigrant status as soon as possible?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in very general terms, regarding citizens of China who might indicate their desire to stay in Canada, we would respond to those cases in the most sympathetic way.
It has been the practice of Secretaries of State for External Affairs for some time not to comment on specific questions regarding events relating to personnel of embassies or consulates, and I think it would be wise for me to respect that practice.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Solicitor General, I direct my question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Yesterday at the Justice Committee, the Director of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service refused to confirm or deny the presence in Canada of the MSS, the Chinese security intelligence service. The Director, however, was prepared to confirm the presence in Canada of other hostile foreign intelligence services. I would submit that the Government has an obligation and indeed a duty to be forthright in this matter.
Is the Secretary of State for External Affairs aware whether or not the MSS, the Chinese intelligence service, is operating in Canada?
Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External
Affairs): Mr. Speaker, I paid particular attention to the testimony of the Director of CSIS yesterday. He indicated that the service keeps an eye on the situation concerning the Chinese community in Canada. Any
June 16, 1989

undeclared intelligence operation in Canada by foreign intelligence services is unacceptable and it will be dealt with by appropriate authorities.
CSIS is responsible for investigations against national security. It reports to the Government which takes the appropriate action that it deems necessary. I can add that in light of the unusual interest and circumstances here, I would be prepared to arrange a briefing for the Leader of the Opposition and the Leader of the New Democratic Party or a Member of Parliament each would designate early in the new week to deal with matters that might arise in these circumstances. I think they would be better dealt with in that way.

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the Director of CSIS was being somewhat selective in that all Canadians, including those who may be at risk, have a right to know whether Chinese intelligence officers are gathering intelligence in Canada. Let there be no mistake. We are dealing with a callous and brutal regime with no concept of due process and with the capability of committing the most heinous crimes against humanity.
I put my question again to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Is he aware of the presence in Canada of these intelligence officers, and if he is not, will he inquire and give the House his undertaking that he will declare these people persona non grata and take immediate steps to have them removed from Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I would add only two things to what I said in my earlier response.
First, I raised with the Chinese Ambassador yesterday allegations with respect to activities that would be improper by officials of his embassy or consulate, and he denied that those activities were occurring. I can report that fact.
The second point I would make is that the Hon. Member has been with me in India and in eastern Europe in circumstances that were sensitive. He comported himself on those occasions in an entirely commendable way, recognizing that there are sometimes circumstances that should await discussion. I would hope
Oral Questions
that he would conform to that high standard here before the television cameras of the House of Commons.

subsubtopic: CONTAMINATION OF CRUSTACEANS IN HOWE SOUND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of the Environment. As he will know, in British Columbia last night, members of the public were advised to no longer eat shrimp, crab or prawns taken from the entire Howe Sound area as well as the Prince Rupert area. I wonder if the Minister would advise the House what other species along the coast of British Columbia have elevated levels of dioxin and organochlorines. Would he also tell the House when the Government first learned that the levels of dioxin and organochlorines in crab, shrimp and prawns in Howe Sound exceeded safe levels for human consumption?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
subsubtopic: CONTAMINATION OF CRUSTACEANS IN HOWE SOUND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member will know that the Government is conducting a sampling program all over Canada to examine and identify the level of dioxins and furans at the exits of paper mills. The data is being collected. It was being examined and analyzed by different Departments. When the analysis was known at the Department of National Health and Welfare, all other Departments were notified of the situation and a decision was made immediately by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans to close those fisheries.

Mr. Speaker, as the Minister knows from a report that was completed last July and was sat on by the Government for more than six months, there are still 17 out of 23 B.C. pulp mills that are in significant non-compliance with their existing licences, and 17 of the 23 are acting in direct violation of the Fisheries Act of Canada.
I wonder if the Minister would tell the House when the Government plans to bring forward regulations and enforcement procedures so that there will be zero discharge of these kinds of toxic, life-endangering toxins into the environment of British Columbia. When will the regulations and enforcement procedures be brought forward? The overwhelming majority of pulp mills, not only in British Columbia but right across Canada, are

June 16, 1989
Oral Questions
violating their licenses and are in direct violation of Canadian law.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, concerning pulp and paper mill pollution, the action of the Government is twofold.
First, there is the furan and dioxin problem, and this is regulated under CEPA. As of now, we are devising veiy tough and comprehensive regulations, that should be put into force next year. For the rest of the pollution, it is regulated under the Fisheries Act and the actual regulations were enacted in 1971 and apply only to mills built after 1971. The majority of mills were built before 1971 and do the most polluting. We have to deal with a situation that goes back more than 18 years.
In two or three years we will be able to issue and enact a new set of regulations for the other kinds of toxic materials exiting from paper mills, but those will be comprehensive regulations applying to all existing mills, built before or after 1971.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister does not seem to understand. This is one of the largest and most widely used fishery areas in all of Canada. More than 400,000 recreational anglers make use of the Howe Sound area. Shrimp, prawn and crab fisheries have now been closed. British Columbians have been told as of 11 o'clock last night to no longer consume any of those products.
The Minister has not told us what other species have elevated levels. Would the Minister at least tell us when, on what precise date, there will be zero discharge regulations and enforcement procedures put in place? What steps does the Government plan to take today to compensate those boats that are now tied up with their crab pods, prawn traps and shrimp pods tied on board? What is the Government going to do, nothing?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government has taken very stringent measures. We have closed fisheries where we have been advised by the Department of National Health and Welfare that the levels of furans and dioxins were too high. We cannot be more drastic. We have stopped the fishing of those species. For the rest, there will be very tough new regulations as early as next year. The Hon.
Member knows very well that the issuance of new regulations as global and complicated as those take a few months, and it will be done no later than 1990.

Mr. Speaker, there are over 2,000 Chinese Canadians in my riding. In the past four days, I have interviewed 700 people of Chinese descent due to the current crisis in China. Because of peaceful pro-democratic demonstrations of the students here in Canada, their parents are under House arrest in China.
Will the Secretary of State for External Affairs send his strongest condemnation of this type of harassment of Canadian residents to the Chinese Government and ask that those being held under house arrest in China be released immediately?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question and for his active interest in the matter. It is entirely helpful that he and other Members of all Parties in the House are in close and active contact with members of the Chinese community in Canada. I conveyed that view yesterday to the Ambassador in my meeting with him.
There is obviously a difference of view between Canadian authorities and Chinese authorities as to what the facts are. There is no doubt in the minds of Chinese authorities that Canada finds any actions of that kind unacceptable. I have asked that that view be conveyed to Chinese authorities.

subtopic: WORK PERMITS AND VISAS OF CHINESE NATIONALS IN CANADA
WORK PERMITS AND VISAS OF CHINESE NATIONALS IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
In light of the situation in China which may continue for a long time and the fact that only eight-week extension visas are being issued to Chinese students and visitors, will the Minister take steps to allow the issuance
June 16, 1989

of work permits and extensions of visas beyond eight weeks?
Will the Minister today announce what concrete steps will be taken to resolve this unfortunate situation? These students need our help, and they need it today.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subtopic: WORK PERMITS AND VISAS OF CHINESE NATIONALS IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we certainly recognize that these students need our help. Perhaps I could clarify for Members exactly what we have done in terms of Chinese citizens currently in Canada, not only students.
Four things can happen that would allow them to remain in Canada: first, to continue in their present status as students, visitors, or temporary workers and sympathetic consideration will be given to extending student or visitor status; seek permanent residence on compelling humanitarian grounds; submit a regular immigration application at a Canadian consulate in the United States or at a Canadian Embassy or consulate in another country of their choice where normal criteria would apply; or submit a refugee claim.
Because there is such great concern about this matter, we will be putting out a package this afternoon in the form of a press release of the detailed information of steps that Chinese citizens in Canada can take.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I, too, have a large Chinese population in my riding.
As protesters in China begin to face arrest, trial, and even death, Chinese citizens on visas here are increasingly concerned about their future. I know of a number of those students in Canada who are convinced that because of their activities it is now impossible for them to return to China.
I ask the Secretary of State: Will the Government be moving beyond its present program of visa renewals and no removals and bringing forward a special program to grant Chinese citizens in Canada landed immigrant status?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CHINESE NATIONALS IN CANADA-LANDED IMMIGRANT STATUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague the Minister has just indicated in the House a series of measures that the Government has already taken.
The Hon. Member will know that the Prime Minister stated some days ago in Vancouver that we will not be sending persons back to danger in China.
The Hon. Member will also know that there is a process under way now in which we are re-evaluating several aspects of our policy, whether it relates to Chinese citizens who are here or whether it relates to the general question of Canada's relations with China. We are proceeding with that as quickly as possible but also in a way that is as careful and comprehensive as possible.
In addition, with regard to the particular situation of students, a meeting will be held this afternoon, a consultation initiated by the Government of Canada, involving representatives of provincial Governments and non-governmental organizations that is designed to look particularly at the problems faced by Chinese students in this country.
Out of that I expect two groups will emerge. One will be an advisory panel available to give advice on any questions which may cause concern to those students. The second is an assistance panel that will be seeking ways-financial assistance, perhaps employment opportunities and other ways-that can contribute materially to the capacity of those persons to stay in Canada.
If Hon. Members have practical suggestions that the Government should be considering to deal with the type of problem quite properly raised by the Hon. Member, we will certainly look at them in a most positive way.

Our officials will also be involved in the meeting this afternoon with the NGOs and the provinces, in order to expedite the situation and to assist with any further measures that we might take.
We will continue to work very closely with the private sector, the community, and the Department of External Affairs on future measures.
However, there is more than one step, and I do want to make that clear. There is more than one thing that can be done, and that is why we will be issuing this package.

Mr. Speaker, earlier today I gave to the Minister of Finance a series of figures showing that between 1982 and 1988 Canada's chartered banks yanked $9 billion out of their business loans portfolio in Alberta. This 50 per cent claw-back by the banks cost Alberta between 100,000 and 140,000 jobs and countless business enterprises.
Why did the Government do nothing while the chartered banks threw literally half of their business loans portfolio overboard?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is putting a somewhat pejorative interpretation on those numbers. I thank him very much for giving me notice of his question.
What has happened since 1982 up to 1988 is that we have seen a significant shift in the relationship in the bank loans to Alberta relative to the rest of the country. At that time the proportion of loans to Alberta was twice the size of its proportionate size in the economy, 25 per cent of business loans as opposed to its share of the GDP, the national income, of 12 per cent.
During this period of time that has come into line, so that it is roughly about the same proportions in both business loans and in its share of the economy.
That is partly as a result of the change in the resource sector. In the resource sector I understand that the loans are down from $10.8 billion to $5.6 billion as the result of a change from a very powerful and very strong period at that time and a number of loans related to takeovers related to the National Energy Program. That has worked its way out of the system, and there has obviously been an impact on other loans as well.

Mr. Speaker, in fact, what has happened has been virtually restricted to the banks. At the same time as they were gutting their Alberta business loans portfolio, local financial institutions such as the credit unions, the mortgage loan companies, and the trust companies when they were going through a difficult period in Alberta, increased their asset base in Alberta. It is only the banks that have abandoned their Alberta portfolios.
In fact, it is not only the resource sector. In that category of loans under $5 million there has been a 33 per cent decline in the bank business loans portfolio in Alberta.
The Minister has responsibility for banking in this country. It is not something that the provincial Government can do. Will he put what pressure he can on the chartered banks to reverse this disastrous policy on behalf of the businesses and the people of Alberta?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member asks what we will do to change this matter. In fact what we did was change the National Energy Program, which was a very large factor in the disastrous impact on the resource sector itself.
That is not true.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member says that it is not true. He should go to speak to people in the resource industry in Alberta. They will say that yes we did kill the National Energy Program. Yes, they will say that this was a good thing for the resource sector. Yes, they will also say that it is setting the stage

for a healthy resource sector in the future, and that is in place right now.
I was going to say that the Hon. Member might be interested, but clearly he is not listening. I should also say that I have spoken to members in the banking community over the course of the last couple of years because I have been aware of this drop taking place. They advised me that the relationship between the size of the Alberta economy and the size of the bank loans is now coming into balance. They expect to see a more normal relationship in the future.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. As of yesterday morning, the External Affairs 1-800 number for Chinese nationals was not offering assistance in any of the Chinese languages. Today, many Chinese in Canada are panicking because the line is constantly busy.
Will the Minister add more lines to this information number? Will he also arrange to have persons who are fluent in the various languages to facilitate the flow of information to a very frightened people?

The fact is that throughout the operation of our hot line we have had operators available to speak to callers in both Mandarin and Cantonese. They have not been answering the telephone in Mandarin or in Cantonese. They have been answering in French or English, but that capacity has always been there on the hot line.
There had been a decrease in the use of the 1-800 number and for that reason the number of hot lines had been reduced. I will see if our information corresponds with that provided by the Hon. Member. If there is a need for new hot lines, they will be installed.

I thank the Minister for his answer. I am sure that he will act on it.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the same Minister. Fear and intimidation are constant within the various Chinese communities in Canada right now, as have been expressed in my riding of Halifax and across the country.
Will the Minister outline for the House what steps his Department is taking to alleviate this fear among Chinese nationals in Canada and to increase their protection in this time of peril and need?
Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External
Affairs): Mr. Speaker, I have raised some of the concerns that are at the root of most of that apprehension directly with the Chinese Ambassador because there have been allegations of names being taken, photographs being used, and harassment being practised.
The views of Canada have been conveyed, the fact that this is utterly unacceptable to us has been conveyed. We will take a range of other measures. I will tiy to make available to Members of the House a precise listing of not only things that have been done but more particularly of people who can be consulted in the event there is a difficulty.
May I make this point: the Department of External Affairs and the Government will do everything we can. I think that one of the most helpful developments has been that to my knowledge Members of Parliament of all Parties across this country, in whose constituencies there are Canadians of Chinese origin or Canadian citizens, have been actively in touch with those persons. I would encourage that to continue.
It is one thing for the Government to be available and to have its services available, but it is far more helpful for Members of Parliament, in our own constituencies, to make it known that if there is anyone with a concern they should come to the Member of Parliament and the Government of Canada. If information reaches me that is accurate and on which we can act, we will act.

June 16, 1989

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Transport, I would like to direct my question to the Minister of State for Transport.
In 1985, the Deputy Prime Minister promised the Mayor of Saint John that his Government would not shut down VIA Atlantic if 200,000 passengers used it by 1990.
In 1988, 240,000 passengers have used the VIA Atlantic route and the figures for the first quarter of this year show an increase of 23 per cent. Clearly, the people of Atlantic Canada have lived up to their end of the deal.
I want to ask the Minister if she will promise that the Government will keep up its end of the deal.

Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of Transport and myself have stated in this House earlier, the decisions relating to VIA will be made once we have received the plan from them, hopefully at the end of this month or early into July. At that time all facts will be taken into consideration and decisions will be made.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport has said that only 3 per cent of Canadians use VIA. According to Transport Canada, most people travel by car. Of those who do not, 20 per cent use VIA; 40 per cent fly; and 40 per cent take the bus. That is the real situation.
Will the Minister read her own Department's figures? Will she do the honourable thing and let VIA provide the service it is capable of and that Canadians have come to expect?

Mr. Speaker, we always do the honourable thing. We make our decisions based on facts and figures.
As the Minister of Transport stated, there are only 3 per cent of Canadians that use the train. VIA is a national service. Three per cent of Canadians nationally use VIA. When the decisions are made, they will be made on the facts that are presented to us by VIA's
studies and its financial plan that it will give to us at the end of June.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice. It relates to election expenses. In the committee yesterday, Jean Marc Hamel, the Chief Election Officer for Canada, indicated that we need some laws to restrict third party advertising during elections.

compliance with the obligations that we have undertaken. However, there is no question that more must be done.

The Minister will know that late yesterday evening there was a very substantial fire in Winnipeg, in St. Boniface, but it is also of concern to the people of Winnipeg-Transcona because the plume of smoke from the fire blew over the northeast end of Winnipeg.
Will the Minister of the Environment tell us whether federal officials, federal inspectors are on the site now? subsubtopic: ST. BONIFACE FIRE-PRESENCE OF FEDERAL INSPECTORS
