speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, May 26, consideration of the motion of Mrs. Landry that Bill C-10, an Act relating to the forgiveness of debts incurred or assumed in respect of certain official development assistance loans made by the Government of Canada to the governments of certain countries in sub-Saharan Africa, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: FORGIVENESS OF DEBTS (SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Resuming debate with the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de Grace.

subtopic: FORGIVENESS OF DEBTS (SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Bill C-10 is to partially forgive
the debts owed to Canada by certain sub-Saharan African countries. It is satisfying to note that the countries of the world are finally giving some attention to this most critical and serious problem of Third World debt.
I say finally because I can recall attending international conferences at the United Nations and elsewhere only four and five years ago when representatives from Latin America and Africa pleaded with representatives of northern and western countries to pay more attention to the developing crises in their countries as a result of the overwhelming debt owed to the North.
Very little was done at first. Perhaps this was due to the fact that at that time the officials and the ministers dealing with the problem in northern and western countries were principally Ministers of Finance and officials in departments of finance. But finally, people who are involved in external affairs and in development assistance have become involved and we have seen some movement. While no problems have been solved yet, at least attention is being given to this extremely serious matter.
We saw in Toronto last summer at the Economic Summit decisions taken to reschedule sub-Saharan African debt. These proposals went forward in the form of the Paris Club plan for a rescheduling of that debt. Then this March, we saw the new Secretary of the Treasury for the United States, Mr. Brady, making additional proposals toward a solution of these debt problems with particular reference to Latin America.
It is heartening to note that Members of Parliament are also getting involved. I had the good fortune to attend a conference organized by Parliamentarians for Global Action, a parliamentary association which is active in this Parliament. This was a conference which this global association of parliamentarians organized at the end of March in Amsterdam, Holland.
At that conference, we had Members of Parliament from most of the G-7 countries and from all political parties. From Canada we had Conservative and Liberal Members. From the European countries, we had Christian Democrats, Social Democrats, radicals, et cetera, with officials and experts discussing how we might on a multi partisan basis deal with the problem of Third World debt. I am pleased to report as well that in this House, for the last few days the Standing Committee on
June 16, 1989

External Affairs and International Trade has been paying special attention to this problem.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, this problem of Third World debt is extremely serious and destabilizing for world peace. What is particularly upsetting, when we look at the facts, is that many of these countries are paying back to creditor countries in the north, countries like the United States and Canada and the western European countries, more in the form of interest than those countries are paying in development assistance. What nonsense, Mr. Speaker.
We have countries in the north boasting about their programs for development assistance on how much they give to African and Latin American countries through their development assistance programs. Yet, on the other hand, those same countries are forced to pay, in the form of debt and interest, moneys back to those very same countries so that in many cases those countries are debt receivers. The northern countries receive more from those poor developing countries than they are giving in assistance.
Let me cite some figures. According to the World Bank, developing country debt now exceeds $1.3 trillion. That is hard to imagine. I can think in terms of millions and billions of dollars, however, when we get into trillions it is very difficult to imagine. But that is now the total debt figure-at least it was at last report-for developing country debt. That is $1.3 trillion.
By the way, the $1.3 trillion is in U.S. dollars. These developing countries have transferred $85 billion U.S. dollars to developed countries since 1982. In the cases of the most highly indebted, this translates to more than 2 per cent of the Gross Domestic Product in the period.
If we can put this in other terms, in recent years the net transfer of capital from the Third World to the rich countries has taken place in large amounts. There has been a net transfer from the Third World, from the poorer countries, to the rich countries. Between 1981 and 1985, net capital export from Latin America moved from U.S. $0.2 billion to U.S. $42.4 billion.
In Asia, the transfer was from $1.7 billion in 1981 to $9.7 billion in 1985. In Africa, from $5.3 billion in 1981 to $21.5 billion in 1985. It is obvious that this makes a farce of our development assistance programs and our philosophy for development assistance.
Forgiveness of Debts Act
If we look at sub-Saharan Africa, which is the main focus of this Bill before the House today, the total outstanding debt of the countries of sub-Saharan Africa at the end of 1985-and that is the most recent report that I have-is about $100 billion. About $100 billion at the end of 1985. The International Monetary Fund estimates $76 billion, excluding arrears of at least $11.6 billion.
In sub-Saharan Africa, the countries most indebted are Nigeria, with $16.6 billion; the Sudan, $7.7 billion; the Ivory Coast, $7.4 billion and Zaire, $4.6 billion. I could go on and on. These debts and the repayment of the debts and the schedule for repayment is extremely important, not only for the suffering and hardship in those countries but also because it is a destabilizing factor in world peace and world politics.
The foreign debts of those countries have been estimated to be the major cause of depression in those countries in the 1980s. Since 1980, many developing countries have experienced a depression more severe than the Great Depression of the 1930s in the industrialized world. The three post-war decades of slow improvement in the living standards of these peoples is such that these developing countries have begun to go backwards. While there had originally been some improvement, now there is backward movement.
This is not only a question of the situation of the peoples in these countries. It is also a question of stability and humanity with respect to those areas. It is sad to note that since 1945, which was the end of the Second World War-which we talk of as the last war, which in fact it was not-there have been 125 wars in which 30 million people have been killed, two-thirds of those people being citizens as compared with one-third military, and three-quarters of those wars have been in the developing world.
In the developing world, there is depression, instability and debt. That is why we have to consider the problem of world debt not simply as a financial and economic question but also a question that affects the whole world. It is a question of peace. When we deal with questions of war and peace, we do not simply look at the number of weapons and nuclear arms involved, we have to look at the causes which lie behind conflict. One of the causes

June 16, 1989
Forgiveness of Debts Act
which lie behind conflict is the severe poverty that exists in many of these countries.
Bill C-10, the Bill before us today, forgives the debt with respect to certain sub-Saharan countries in Africa, 13 countries which are listed in the annex to the Bill. While it does not solve the problem, it is certainly a move in the right direction. My hon. colleague, our Party's critic, has pointed out some of the shortcomings in the Bill.
Today I appeal to Canadians to understand and support the reasons which lie behind a Bill like this. When I happen to meet some people in the street, they ask why we are forgiving the debts of African countries. People ask why we do not do this for Canadians, why we do not forgive the debts of Canadian farmers and business people instead of forgiving the debts of these African countries. In Canada, we do have very significant programs to deal with this, though they are not enough. We on this side criticize the Government for not doing enough, but there are programs like Old Age Security, the Canadian Pension Plan, certain regional development programs, the Canadian Assistance Plan, Medicare and the like, programs at the federal and provincial levels that deal with the problems of Canadians. As well, there is a Bankruptcy Act in Canada. We have insolvency legislation so that when people get into debt over their heads, they can get out of that debt and start all over again. We do not drive them into the ground and let them starve to death. We have legislative means for helping them. Unfortunately, in the international arena that is not the case.
When countries like Brazil, Argentina and Peru have debts with banks in Canada, the United States, Britain, France and Germany, there is no international Bankruptcy Act that would allow these countries to get back on their feet again. If we believe in the philosophy of bankruptcy and insolvency legislation for those who live within our own national boundaries, we should translate that spirit into the international arena and should be ready to forgive debts in certain cases which would drive the country to what I would call complete insolvency. That is what some of the proposals that are now on the table are attempting to do. I am referring to the decisions taken at the Toronto Economic Summit last summer where a plan was put forward for rescheduling
certain Third World debt, known as the Paris Club for debt rescheduling. It is certainly not enough. It will not solve the problems, but at least it is a beginning and a move in the right direction.
On March 10, U.S. Treasury Secretary, Nicholas Brady, a member of the new Bush Government in the United States, unveiled a plan in which he exhorted commercial banks to forgive a portion of their Third World loans in return for guarantees that at least some of the debt would be paid. One would think that would be looked on with reason and with a long term view. Unfortunately, some of the banks, including some Canadians banks, have not been too sympathetic to that proposal.
A certain number of parliamentarians met in Amsterdam at the end of March, and I was one of them. We met at a conference organized by Parliamentarians for Global Action and after two and a half days of discussion, we put out a document entitled,"The Amsterdam Appeal". In that appeal, we stated:
We agreed that the recent new debt relief policies-although moving in a more positive direction-are insufficient and need substantial extension. In fact, the new debt strategy requires a "Toronto plus" and a "Brady plus" approach. The debtor countries require both debt reduction and new concessional finance as a pre-condition though not a substitute for valid and sound domestic economic policies. Funds for debt policies reduction should be additional to those already allocated for aid.
Then we made certain specific recommendations, some with respect to Latin American countries whose debt is principally commercial and is owed to creditor banks in the northern hemisphere. We made other recommendations with respect to the sub-Saharan countries whose debt is principally with governments of countries in the north. Since the Bill we are dealing with today focuses on the sub-Saharan African countries and their govemment-to-govemment debts, let me mention some of the recommendations that were made.
We said again that the Toronto Summit set an important precedent by authorizing debt reduction in connection with rescheduling in the Paris Club, and we said that the need of African and other low-income countries for external resource flows and debt reduction has not yet, however, been adequately addressed. We recommended first that there be a write-down of a significant portion of the Paris Club debt. Second, we recommended that
June 16, 1989

there be a moratorium of 10 years on all official interest and principal payment obligations.
Further, we recommended that the budgetary costs of these debt reductions be added to aid donor commitments and not be taken from existing aid allocations. That is very important because the existing aid allocations are being relied upon for certain projects in Third World countries and to simply take some of those moneys for the debt reduction would not solve the problem. We also recommended that aid donors who have not already done so plan a program of cancellation of their aid-related debts and, through this Bill, there is the cancellation of certain debts. Finally, a very interesting recommendation made by the parliamentarians in Amsterdam is that the International Monetary Fund consider the sale of a portion of its gold holdings to finance additional multilateral concessional lending to low-income, debt-distressed countries.
These are some of the proposals made by parliamentarians, experts, financial people and businessmen to try to resolve these important problems. In conclusion, I would like to make an appeal to Canadian citizens to understand how serious the poverty is in these countries of Africa and Latin America. We must reach out to them to do things which will support them in the development of their peoples and countries. I recall how Canadians and people from all over the world responded a few years ago when they saw on television the starving children in Ethiopia. They responded with great heart and gave in substantial amounts. They gave through rock concerts and in many other ways. That was because they saw very graphically on television how horrible the situation was. It has not gone away. The fact that we do not see it on television every day does not mean that it has gone away. It is still there in Latin America. It is still there is Asia and in Africa.
I urge the Canadian people to support our Government and urge it to do more in order that we can have a world where there is co-operation between peoples and not conflict and war.

subtopic: FORGIVENESS OF DEBTS (SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate. As the previous speaker indicated, I would like to suggest that it is a step in the right direction.
Bill C-10 on which we are completing discussion today is a Bill that forgives the govemment-to-govemment debt that a number of sub-Saharan countries have with the Government of Canada.
It is important to recognize those countries as identified in the Bill. They are the Republic of Camaroon, the People's Republic of the Congo, Republic of the Ivory Coast, Gabonese Republic, Republic of Ghana, Republic of Kenya, Democratic Republic of Madagascar, Federal Republic of Nigeria, Republic of Senegal, Kingdom of Swaziland, Republic of Zaire, Republic of Zambia and Republic of Zimbabwe.
This at least is a recognition by the Government of the incredibly bleak conditions that face the people in those sub-Saharan countries. Time and time again we are reminded as Canadians, normally through the news media, of the terrible conditions that exist for the people in those countries. We are not reminded every day because those terribly horrible conditions are not news, as we normally define news. They are on occasion flashed on our television screens or covered in various publications. For the people of the sub-Saharan, and generally people of developing countries, these terrible conditions go on day after day, year after year, decade after decade.
As parliamentarians, we are aware of those situations. Over the years we have urged the Government of Canada to take appropriate steps. That is why today it is fair to say that on a government-to-govemment basis steps are being taken. We support this particular initiative to at least ease some of the debt burden that those countries have in terms of debts they owe to the Government of Canada as a result of a variety of aid packages and aid loans over the years.
However, it is important that we now go beyond this. While we say that this is a step in the right direction and as a result of this initiative that we are passing in Bill C-10 a small amount of the debt faced by those countries will be eliminated, it is only the tip of the iceberg in terms of the iceberg being the problem. The tremendous

June 16, 1989
Forgiveness of Debts Act
debt problems those countries face is something that I do not believe Canadians are able to easily comprehend. I say that for two reasons.
When we in our country get into serious debt problems, either as individuals, as organizations, or as businesses, we have legislation that recognizes that from time to time this does occur, often through no fault of the players but because of changing circumstances. For example, a farm that might be struggling through difficult financial or climactic times may find itself in a bankruptcy situation. Often when people find themselves with a serious debt problem, it is not necessarily because of their inability to deal with the financial challenges that face them, but is as a result of outside circumstances that create this debt situation to a point where repayment of the debt is simply impossible.
In our country when that occurs to individuals, businesses, organizations, we have backruptcy and insolvency legislation to deal with that in order to attempt to recognize that steps must be taken to pay off, as much as possible, those to whom the money is owed. But we are not in a position to drive those individuals into starvation, or literally to destroy the lives of the people and their families involved. We have taken on a rather humane view of financial crises that individuals, groups and, companies experience.
That same logic and goodwill ought now to be extended to the developing countries. When one looks at the plight that they are in, at the incredible financial and economic challenges faced by them, in most cases those challenges have nothing to do with the people themselves but are foisted upon them from outside.
We all recognize that as a result of a variety of forces, the sub-Saharan countries have faced incredible drought problems. Rural and particularly nomadic peoples have been forced to move off their traditional lands and focus their activities in certain areas, and as a result overgrazing and desert expansion results. It seems that the natural environment that has sustained previous generations for hundreds and thousands of years simply evaporated overnight as a result of desert conditions extending into the sub-Saharan area day by day.
If we were honest, we would all recognize that the developed countries, the First World and the Second World countries as we define them, have exploited the
Third World countries, the Fourth World countries and the developing countries for years and years. They have gone in and extracted their natural resources and taken advantage of the desperate situation in which the people find themselves and have exploited the people in a variety of ways.
We do not have to look any further than the so-called free trade zones on the American-Mexican border where people are working for a few cents a day. Those same people working in a country such as Canada would be paid $7 or $8 an hour. That is the reality. We have exploited those people in these countries for decades.
Now those countries find themselves in a desperate situation financially. We have to ask what our response has been. By "our" response I do not necessarily refer to the Government of Canada directly, but I do indirectly, because it involves our chartered banks that operate overseas, it involves organizations such as the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund, organizations of which we are a part. The answer that those organizations have placed on those countries is to impose what can only be described as a new right concept in terms of applying market-place forces on those countries and asking them to cut back on important government services in terms of developing urban and economic infrastructure, cut back on education, cut back on health care, and cut back on housing. In other words, imposed a veil of poverty and starvation on the people of those countries. That is the reality. We can couch it in all manner of fancy economic terms.
Recently, not in the sub-Saharan but in Venezuela, some pointy-headed bureaucrats who sit in Washington, D.C. making decisions on behalf of the IMF have suggested an incredibly oppressive package be placed on that country. That country has been given no alternative because it needed a carry-over loan because of the tremendous debt situation it is experiencing.
The International Monetary Fund stated that it would loan Venezuela the money to cany it over the next number of months, if it imposed upon its people a harsh and cruel program of restraint. That country was given no alternative. We saw rioting in the streets as the gas prices were increased significantly and people had to abandon their cars because they simply could not afford the cost of gasoline. They then had to depend on a public
June 16, 1989

transportation system which was already overburdened in some of the major cities, and whole cities ended up in chaos. There was rioting, killing, looting and burning as a result of the poorest of the country being the hardest hit. That decision was made by pointy-headed bureaucrats sitting in the United States with no understanding of the political, cultural and economic reality of those Third World countries, and no sensitivity.
We are part of that process. Canada, being a participant in the IMF and a player in the World Bank decisions, would have an opportunity to influence some of those decisions. When we look at the whole process of structural adjustment that the IMF, the World Bank, and the banks in the other developing countries are imposing on these developing countries, no wonder they are ending up virtually worse off as a result of this so-called adjustment.
I think it is only fair to say that adjustment becomes more intelligible when understood as a technology of control. What First World countries have determined is that our way of life in countries like the United States, Canada, and Western Europe ought to be imposed on the developing countries regardless of their culture, the realities of their economies, their traditions, or their social values. We are going to impose what has worked in our country on theirs.
We must recognize that what has worked and resulted in the prosperity that we experience today in countries like Canada, the United States and Western Europe is a result of exploitation of Third World countries. It goes right back to the very beginning with the Conquistadors going into Latin America and extracting, in a barbaric way, the resources back to Spain. We see the same thing here in terms of the reaction to exploitation of our native people through the fur trade from the very beginning of the Canadian economy.
We have to admit that our prosperity, wealth and lifestyle, of which we are veiy proud, to a certain extent in some cases and to a large extent in other cases, is based on the exploitation of people in the developing countries. So there is no way that we can impose our system of exploitation now focused on them because there is no one left to exploit. They cannot apply the
Forgiveness of Debts Act
same methods and technology of exploitation to those around them.
It is an unrealistic solution. Canada can make a difference in the international community, particularly as we participate in these international organizations that are making the decisions to impose this new right solution called "Structural Adjustment" on the people of the developing countries.
In conclusion, I want to say that we certainly do support this initiative. It is, hopefully, not an empty initiative that simply gives the impression that Canada is concerned.
I have spoken about the fact that while we might make some small concessions in terms of govemment-to-gov-emment loans due Canada by tearing up those papers requiring that loan repayment, we fail on two other counts that I think we have to recognize. There is one I have just mentioned in terms of our participation in organizations such as the International Monetary Fund. Also, how serious are we in developing and supporting the economy of the sub-Saharan countries?
The way we evaluate the Government's concern is by what we do with our overseas development assistance programs. Do we extend additional assistance to those countries in desperate need? Do we look at the developing country and identify new ways and means of supporting its efforts toward self-reliance and self-determination? I am afraid it is a very sad day for the Government of Canada to have to admit that, no, we are reducing our commitments.
As a matter of fact, during the last Budget, that section of the Budget that had the deepest, most wicked and cruel cuts, was that of overseas development. CIDA, one of the arms of our foreign aid work has made a tremendous difference in terms of changing, on a relatively small scale, the local economies in terms of developing people's basic training and skills, developing local infrastructure to allow people to develop self-determination and self-reliance. This Government has curtailed large expenditures in those areas. After all, the proof of the pudding is in the eating.
We can stand here for days and listen to government Members talk about their concern for the Third World and their interest in assisting Third World economic development. The reality is that we should be prepared to put our dollars to assist in those initiatives. I am sad to say that the reality is that the Government says, no, we

I say it is a sad day. While we see this Bill as a signal that perhaps the Government has come to its senses and recognized the responsibilities and obligations we have internationally, let us hope that we will see a change in attitude in terms of the amount of money we put into official overseas assistance. Mr. Speaker, I do not withdraw anything that I said.
Forgiveness of Debts Act
To get on with the debate at hand, it concerns the forgiveness of debts in the sub-Saharan regions. I want to go on record with my colleague, the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand), in saying that my Party concurs with the principle of what this Bill is trying to do. In our concurrence, however, we do not thoroughly agree with everything that is being done, but we believe that we are on the right track in terms of the forgiveness of debt in these particular countries.
I wish to try to put a more human face on the debate and what is going on in Africa now. Three months ago I had occasion to have a luncheon with the Minister of Health for the Sudan. She had been visiting Canada along with her brother. They spoke to a number of parliamentarians here on Parliament Hill. They were telling us about the state of health of the people but, more particularly, of the children of the Sudan which left us very near to tears.
A few years ago I was in Washington. I overheard a conversation between two representatives of farmers' groups from a country called Lower or Upper Volta, I am not sure which. They were talking about mechanizing in their country, mechanizing in order to bring forth better crops. Since I have a farm implement dealer factory in my riding, I was pretty much interested in what kind of machinery they were using. They were talking about mechanization and the fact that they were at last going to get, I think, a horse or a donkey rather than having the children and the wife pull the ploughs. We are dealing here with countries which are not only underdeveloped but which about I think it would be fair to say lack even the basic tools to feed themselves.
In this debate I would like to put a human face on Bill C-10 and what is happening in Africa. For almost 900 million people, approximately one-sixth of mankind, the march of human progress has now become, in my opinion, a retreat. In many nations development is being thrown into reverse. After decades of steady economic advance, large areas of the world are sliding backward into more abysmal poverty.
Throughout most of Africa, average incomes have fallen by 10 per cent to 25 per cent in the 1980s. In the 37 poorest nations, spending per person on health has been reduced by 50 per cent and on education by 25 per cent over the last few years.

June 16, 1989
Forgiveness of Debts Act
In almost one-half of 103 developing countries from which recent information is available, the proportion of six to eleven-years olds enrolled in primary school is now falling. Not only do they not have the money to take care of themselves in terms of health and food, they cannot even nourish the minds which in the future might get them out of their cycle of poverty. In other words, it is the children who are bearing the heaviest burden of debt and recession of the 1980s. In tragic summary it can be estimated that at least half a million young children have died in the last 12 months as a result of the slowing down or reversal of progress in the developing world.
For most of the countries of Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean, almost every economic signal points to the fact that development has been derailed, per capita GNP has fallen, debt repayments have risen to a quarter or more of all export earnings, share in world trade has dropped and the productivity of labour has declined by one or two percentage points each year throughout the entire 1980s.
It is the young child whose growing mind and body is susceptible to permanent damage from even temporary deprivation. It is the young child whose individual development today and whose social contribution tomorrow is being shaped by the economics now. It is the young child who is paying the highest of all prices and who will bear the most recurring of all costs for the mounting debt repayments, the drop in export earnings, the increase in food costs, the fallen family income, the rundown of health services and the narrowing of educational opportunities.
Too often, spending money on health or education is regarded as a form of consumption which can only be afforded in times of plenty. Protecting the health and education of these children is the basic of all investments in the physical and mental capacity of the next generation and, therefore, in the social and economic development of all societies and, most particularly, in the societies of the sub-Sahara.
It is no longer necessary for approximately 40,000 young children to die every day, every day even as we speak in the developing world, and for so many millions more to live on with ill-health and poor growth. The advances already achieved during the 1980s in immunization, in family spacing and in the drafting of a convention
on the rights of the child are among the great humanitarian achievements of our times, something in which our country has taken a part. However, these are jewels in a tarnished crown. Without restoring the forward momentum of economic development, it will become increasingly difficult to sustain such progress.
Two elements have dominated the deterioration of economic prospects over so much of the developing world in recent years. They are rising debt payments and falling commodity prices.
The total debt of the developing world is now over $1,000 billion U.S. In many countries annual repayment of interest and capital amount to more than the total of all the new aid and loans being received each year. On average, repayments now claim about 25 per cent of the developing world's principal export revenues.
The developing world still depends on raw materials for the majority of its export earnings. However, in the last 10 years real prices for the developing world's principal commodities have fallen by approximately 30 per cent. The fall in new commercial lending and the inadequate and static levels of official aid complete the four walls of the financial prison in which so much of the developing world has been incarcerated during this decade.
In 1979, a net of $40 billion flowed from the northern hemisphere to the developing nations of the south. Today that flow has been reversed. Taking everything into account, loans, aid repayments of interest and capital, the southern world is now transferring at least $20 billion a year to the northern hemisphere. That is a difference of $60 billion which could be used in helping these developing nations. As a result, most of the affected nations have been forced to adopt economic adjustment policies in an attempt to stave off balance of payments crises while at the same time meeting debt obligations, maintaining essential imports and struggling unsuccessfully to return to economic growth.
The need for adjustment is not really in question. The manner of adjustment by contrast is an issue which is both complex and controversial. Now with or without support from the International Monetary Fund, the IMF, adjustment policies have usually taken the form of a dampening down of demand, a devaluation of the currency, a withdrawal of subsidies on fuel and stable food
June 16, 1989

stuffs and deep cuts in Government spending. In total over 70 developing nations are now struggling to adjust their economies by just such methods.
I have here, as an aside, a copy of The Financial Post. This great literary newspaper seems to be in favour of just this type of thing. I know when they are in favour of something like that, it is a very good reason for myself and anyone in the Liberal Party to be against it.
It is the poor and the vulnerable who are suffering the most, and for two main reasons: First, the poor have the least economic "fat" with which to absorb the blow of recession. Often three-quarters of the income of the very poor is spent on food and much of what remains is needed for fuel and water, housing and clothes, bus fares if they have buses and most needed of all, medical treatment. In such circumstances a 25 per cent cut in real incomes obviously means going without even the basic necessities in these countries.
The second reason is that the poor also have the least political muscle to ward off the blow. The services which have been lost or radically pruned are health services, primary education and food and fuel subsidies, the services on which the poor are most dependent and which they have the least opportunity to replace by any other private means.
Over the last decade, for example, the proportion of Government expenditure devoted to health has fallen in most countries of sub-Saharan Africa, in more than half of the countries of Latin-America, in the Caribbean and in one-third of all the nations of Asia. There is little doubt that adjustment strategies are failing in at least two major ways. First, as I have already pointed out, they have placed a disproportionate burden on the poorest and most vulnerable, and the children are those who are the most vulnerable of all.
Second, they have succeeded in a principal aim of allowing indebted economies to escape from debt to return to healthy economic growth. It is this second failure to restore growth which must be urgently addressed in order to protect the poorest and the most vulnerable, and also to contribute to a quickening of economic growth of a kind which smaller and poorer producers could both contribute to and benefit from. Despite the hardships being visited upon the poor, present policies for coping with the debt crisis are
Forgiveness of Debts Act
manifestly not succeeding in restoring economic growth to the most indebted nations.
For sub-Saharan Africa, in particular, the agonies of economic adjustment are evidently not the birth pangs of a new economic growth. Sooner or later the fact will have to be faced that in many countries attempts to pay interest and capital on the full amount of present debts is fundamentally incompatible with return to economic development. That is why at the beginning of my intercession today I said that our Party was in favour of the principle of this particular Bill. Debt payments at present levels may not only reduce consumption and all the human hardship that that implies, but also a reduction in investment and in future economic progress.
I want to quote a few figures from a paper which was written by Mr. John Locksley. In the past two years, it has become apparent that the world debt crisis is not confined to the large debtor countries, and that most African countries are facing debt obligations which they will find very difficult indeed. They are less spectacular than famine, and less threatening to our own financial institutions than debt difficulties elsewhere. The African debt crisis is of daunting proportions. Unless the outside world moves quickly to render assistance, many African countries will experience immense social and economic dislocation and deprivation as they seek to service their debts. That is why this is a good gesture on the part of this Government.
Figures for African debt outstanding are notoriously unreliable, but the International Monetary Fund estimates that they are over $130 billion. This figure has more than doubled in the last 10 years. It is now the equivalent of 150 per cent of the whole continent's total annual exports or 30 per cent of its total GDP. The debt of sub-Saharan African countries is equal to 230 per cent of exports and to 68 per cent of GDP figures which are well in excess of even the large problem debtors, the difficulties of which are so well documented.
The annual costs of servicing this huge debt have risen sharply from $3,6 billion in 1978 to over $15 billion today. Over the same period, Africa's export earnings have risen by only $20 billion. The bulk of this increase has been used for what? For bettering the lifestyle of the people there? For bettering their lives? No, for servicing the debt. Annually these commitments now absorb 28

per cent of all the export earnings, the highest for any region of the world outside of Latin-America.
It is apparent that many of these countries will be devoting significant proportions of their income and foreign exchange earnings for debt servicing in the years ahead. The negative consequences of this scenario are likely to be horrendous for the economic and social well-being of the affected peoples, most of whom even without this burden live close to the subsistence level. Their ability to purchase imports, so vital to the operation of their economies, will be severely constrained. This will lead again to unemployment, an excess capacity in industry and trade, a fall in investment and a lack of input into such key areas as agriculture, health and education.
I think that the point has been well made. I think that Members on this side of the House have stated the position of our Party. We are moving in the right direction in this debt forgiveness, but this Government should extend itself even more. It should reconsider, or at least consider in the next budget, and see to it that these people in Africa do not have any more cuts in CIDA, do not have any more cuts at least from this country. We should be opening up our hearts and in this case our purses so that the least fortunate people on this planet can have a chance to survive and live their lives in some kind of dignity.

PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   ENERGY NATURAL GAS EXPORTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the "surplus test" should be restored so that no exports of natural gas from Canada would be permitted unless it could be shown that volumes slated for export were surplus to Canadian needs reasonably projected over the 25-year period following the commencement of the proposed export.
He said: Mr. Speaker, no doubt to the delight of those present here this afternoon, I propose to keep my remarks mercifully brief and to the point.
I would start by noting a couple of things about natural gas and Canadian supply. First, rolling in our non-conventional reserves, which is to say principally those Arctic reserves to which no pipeline has yet been built, we enjoy at current rates of export and domestic consumption about a 25.5-year supply of natural gas in this country. So, there is no question that the matter addressed by the motion is not an urgent one.
However, it should be noted that there are two overwhelming factors that we must constantly keep in mind when we address the question of domestic supply of natural gas. The first is, obviously, Canada is a northern country. We have cold winters. We need to be very careful in the husbanding of those energy resources which allow us to thrive and prosper during those long cold winters.
Second, as we move, for we must move, from excessive dependence on conventional gasoline and such fuels for the powering of our automobiles, the heating of our homes, and the running of our factories and other industry, natural gas will play a crucial transitional role. We will move to energy alternatives. We have no choice. It will happen. But in getting there we will be absolutely reliant on large supplies of natural gas as we move from old technologies to the new.
Those are the two things we should bear in mind in considering this matter. One, that we are a northern country and need energy resources and, two, that natural gas has a crucial environmental role to play in this country. It is in light of this that we should examine what is happening in the export market which currently is
June 16, 1989

most respondent to two overwhelming factors. The first factor is the willy-nilly deregulation of the oil and gas industry undertaken since 1985 and the second is the signing of the Free Trade Agreement with the United States and its implementation as of January 1.
There is no question that that gas bubble in the United States which had kept Canadian exports to that market at such a low level for so long is contracting. Indeed, it can be expected to disappear completely over the next five to ten years. In fact, there are already huge volumes of natural gas under consideration for export to the American market: for example, the applications now before the National Energy Board are for permission to export Arctic gas in volumes unprecedented in Canadian trade with that country. Currently there is nothing in regulation or statute, certainly not under the FTA, to prohibit a rapidly accumulating volume of exports to the United States of Canadian gas. There is no cap or ceiling. It is technically possible that we could wind up in a short period of time exporting 80 per cent of our proved reserves to the United States. I think that is unlikely but my point is that there is nothing in regulation or statute to prevent it. I think that would be a foolish thing to do but not technically impossible.
There is a very large expansion in the capacity of the transmission pipelines to the United States under way now. There are applications for new pipelines to be built and for further expansions of existing pipelines. There is no question that the players in the market are gearing up for greatly expanded exports to the United States,and this in light of what some industry analysts call the "FTA ratchet" which, simply put, is the provision in the Free Trade Agreement that gives the United States the mandate to continue to receive the proportion of our energy resources that the Americans received in the average of the previous three years should some regime of rationing be brought in. This means that as our exports to the United States grow in volume, our ability in the future to close off those exports to some degree is diminished in that we must always be prepared to supply to the Americans the same percentage of production that was in place prior to any rationing.
Natural Gas Exports
In the absence of any regulatory or statutory provision requiring the maintenance of some kind of reserve for Canadian use, we run the risk of signing over huge quantities of our gas reserves to the American market in virtual perpetuity. We may wish to do this. The Government may decide that this is a good and prudent policy. I do not agree but the point is we should understand that if that is the policy decision there will be those consequences.
I think it is prudent, especially in light of the Free Trade Agreement, that we return to a regime whereby a guaranteed supply is retained for Canadian purposes over a prudent period. Twenty-five years was the previous surplus test. It makes sense and is a good policy for Canada to return to that regime. However, I note as well that under the current deregulation regime, the simple imposition of a surplus test only would be grievously unfair to the producers because it would put an overwhelming bargaining tool into the hands of the consumers of the product.
If there were a 25-year surplus test requirement before the producers could sell any volume above that 25-year supply to the United States, it would be a simple matter for the principally-eastem-Canadian consumers to sit back and say: "Fine, you are not selling any of that until you bring the price down to something that we like". It is an easy scenario to envisage and one that I think would ensue almost immediately were we to return to a surplus test regime in the absence of other regulation. This is why I view this motion to be in tandem with other re-regulatory initiatives. We need to re-regulate the price especially with regard to the return to a border price test but as well the return to a regime of regulated pricing generally in Canada.
Is this a proposal for a return to a regulated price that would be bearable in consumer markets and give to the producers of the resource a fair return allowing them to go out and explore further to discover new reserves which, by the way, the current market price does not do?
Is this the thin edge of the wedge in terms of complete re-regulation? The answer, Mr. Speaker, is yes. Unqualifiedly, that is in fact what I am proposing.

Natural Gas Exports
If I may digress just briefly here, I would like to plead with those whose assigned task it is this afternoon to quarrel with this proposal, not to bring up the red herring of the National Energy Program. I realize that this request on my part is in all likelihood doomed to go unmet. But I feel compelled to make it regardless, for the simple reason that what is proposed here has nothing to do with the NEP.
The NEP in its three principal provisions imposed the PGRT, the petroleum gas revenue tax, diverted investment dollars from the western sedimentary basin to the frontier Canada Lands and provided a regime for the progressive Canadianization of the oil and gas industry.
Our government, having slain that particular jabber-wock, "O Frabjous day!", cannot now claim that the return to a regime of regulated pricing, a 25-year surplus test, and the border price test has anything to do with the NEP. All of those factors in fact predate the NEP. They were left unchanged by the NEP. They were done away with, not in consequence of the doing away with the NEP, but in the coincidental elimination of various forms of regulation in the oil and gas industry.
I would argue that de-regulation has been in place long enough for it now to be understood as a grievous error. It has created a situation in which billions of dollars of investment have been drawn out of the Province of Alberta, and to a lesser degree other provinces, in which hundreds of companies have gone out of business, especially the independent Canadian juniors, in consequence of which Canadianization of the industry has been rolled back. We have lost the accumulated skill and expertise of decades in one fell swoop. The rate of the finding of new reserves has dropped to a trickle. The Americans in consequence have been granted a control over our reserves which they could not have dreamed of 20 years ago.
The central fact of the matter is that in Canada it is imprudent and heedless of Canadian history to rely on the market. In Canada, the market must be tamed and put to the purposes of public policy democratically arrived at. We rely on the market at the peril of our nation and to the enhancement of the Americans' nation.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   ENERGY NATURAL GAS EXPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member suggested that we not refer to the NEP. Frankly, I cannot help but refer to it when he speaks of regulated pricing in all forms of the oil and gas
industry. That is precisely what the National Energy Program was for, a Made in Canada oil price.
Earlier today in Question Period, he talked about the banks and how money has been taken away from Alberta. The reason the banks failed was as a direct result of the National Energy Program. Real estate prices fell. Businesses failed. People lost their jobs. At the tail end of a recession there were bank failures.
With this motion and Motion M-97, the Hon. Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Harvey) suggests that we have a floor price. He is advocating the return to a national energy program or a program with similar consequences. Other than to have these few brief comments about the National Energy Program, I will not return to it. I think the Member for Edmonton East will be thankful for that.
Approval of the Hon. Member's motion would not only represent a return to past practice, it would be a step into the past, to the bad old days when the Government of Canada's energy trade policies were based upon notions of hoarding and unfair treatment of trading practices. It would imperil the stable and attractive investment environment that this Government has strived to achieve. Instead of promoting energy security, it would reduce it. It would also seriously affect the prospects for investment, employment and economic growth in Canada.
Since 1984, this Government has undertaken a number of initiatives to improve the health of the energy sector and to restore its vital role in achieving a sound energy and economic future in all regions of the country. Among its principal initiatives, this Government has deregulated oil and gas markets, undertaken regulatory reforms and eliminated unnecessary and onerous restrictions on trade in oil, gas and electricity. It has put in place a more balanced and profit-sensitive fiscal regime to encourage investment and development.
These initiatives were guided by one fundamental principle, that dynamic market forces are the most reliable and efficient means to guide energy production and consumption decisions.
This Government's energy policy has recognized the need to foster the development of Canadian resources and of competitive markets in order to create an environment in which, first, consumers are assured that sufficient and diverse supplies of energy will be available at fair and competitive prices, and second, producers benefit from a wide range of market opportunities and a stable and attractive investment climate. These policies do not mean that the Government has withdrawn from
June 16, 1989

the energy sector scene nor that the Government no longer has a legitimate role to play in energy matters. Quite the contrary.
While the Government's policy emphasizes the valuable role of market forces to guide energy production and consumption decisions, it also recognizes that markets are not always perfect. This Government takes seriously its responsibilities to ensure that the interests of Canadians are protected. The National Energy Board in particular performs an important monitoring and review role to ensure that markets are operating properly-
The existing market based procedure used by the NEB to review natural gas export proposals combines greater reliance on market forces with intervention if and when necessary in order to protect the interests of Canadian consumers and producers.
While the Government's regulatory framework has been streamlined, this is not an indication that it is any less effective. It is only an indication that the previous regulatory regime was terribly excessive, imposing severe costs on the producing industry while not providing any material advantage in terms of energy security for Canadians.
Canadians realize that true energy security cannot be achieved through hoarding. Policies which encourage competitive and responsive energy markets, coupled with appropriate emergency measures and international co-operation, are the most effective means of achieving energy security.
One of the best indicators of how we in Canada co-operate internationally is the Free Trade Agreement. In its simplest terms, the Free Trade Agreement calls for the freest possible bilateral trade in energy. This has been achieved through the elimination or reduction of tariff and non-tariff barriers and an establishment of rules to govern energy trade in the future.
At the same time, the Free Trade Agreement acknowledges the legitimate right of governments to maintain appropriate regulatory systems and to restrict exports when circumstances warrant. This does not mean that the Free Trade Agreement will result in a surge of
Natural Gas Exports
exports above what would normally occur in a deregulated environment. The growth in the energy sector over time and the volume of energy exports to the U.S. or elsewhere will be guided not only by the availability of resources but by the economic opportunities that exist.
Can exports be restricted? Does this mean that Canada can no longer restrict exports to the U.S. or to other foreign markets even if it is in the public interest to do so? Clearly, we can restrict exports.
There are a number of reasons for which the Government might authorize export restrictions, all of which are recognized by the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and the Free Trade Agreement. The Free Trade Agreement includes some conditions that must be observed if the Government chooses to restrict exports in certain circumstances. Two points bear emphasis in this regard. It would rarely, if ever, be in Canada's interests to restrict exports. Restrictive action usually results in reduced revenues for Canadian energy producers, thus reduced incentives to find and develop additional supplies. Restrictions often entail a beggar thy neighbour approach to export customers and provokes strong resistance on the part of the producing provinces, especially Alberta.
Second, exports nonetheless can be restricted for reasons set out in the GATT. These include the existence of a short supply situation, the need to conserve depleting resources and to effect measures taken in connection with a price stabilization program. In other words, the Free Trade Agreement has addressed the Hon. Member's concerns.
If exports are restricted to deal with situations of critical shortages, conservation and in conjunction with price stabilization schemes, the FTA further provides that three conditions must be respected. The first condition is that Governments may not interfere to restrict export customers' competitive access to the share of total supply that they have previously enjoyed. This does not mean that Canada is obligated to supply or deliver that share. It simply means that governments will not interfere with the competitive access up to the allowable limit.

June 16, 1989
Natural Gas Exports
Canadian consumers, on the other hand, will have competitive access to all available supply.
The second condition is that the governments will not discriminate against U.S. customers by imposing higher prices on exports than those charged for domestic sales. Higher export prices may, however, result from competitive market forces. This provision applies only to government action to impose higher prices than those charged to domestic customers.
Finally, governments agree not to act in a manner that will disrupt normal channels of supply or the normal mix of energy products being exported. What is noteworthy about these conditions is that they apply only to exceptional circumstances and apply only to government actions that could otherwise result in arbitrary and discriminatory actions. In other words, they entail a presumption that the competitive operation of market forces will generally produce a better and fairer result than the arbitrary actions of bureaucrats. God knows, we have too many of those.
There are many other reasons for which governments or the NEB may restrict exports legitimately under both the FTA and the GATT. For example, restrictions imposed for the regulation of monopoly, for environmental reasons, for reasons of public safety or to correct the effects of unfair trade practices in the marketplace are all legitimate reasons for which governments might intervene. In these general circumstances, the proportional access provisions which J have outlined do not apply.
It is quite clear that the Hon. Member's motion providing for a return to a surplus test based on the argument that Canada has lost its ability to restrict exports is completely unnecessary.
In summary, let me re-emphasize the main points I have made. The setting aside of 25 years of reserve would run counter to Canada's energy policy which clearly emphasizes the critical role of competitive markets to achieve not only Canada's energy security objectives but also its important economic and regional development objectives. An arbitrary 25-year reserve requirement would impose severe costs on the industry, jeopardize the attractive investment environment in the oil and gas sector, increase federal, provincial and
regional tensions and result in foregone opportunities for expanded trade and economic growth. This will mean fewer jobs for Canadians while we want more jobs, more economic opportunity and a fairer and more just society for Canadians.
Walter Van De Walle (St. Albert): Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in the House to express my confidence in the National Energy Board as the custodian of our Canadian natural gas supplies. The National Energy Board has the sole legislative responsibility to protect reasonably foreseeable domestic natural gas requirements. In my opinion, the board has discharged this responsibility very well in the past, and I see no reason to doubt its capability to do this in the future.
My hon. friend from Edmonton East disagrees with this. He wants a surplus test to be restored, but not just any surplus test. Rather, he wants:
That, in the opinion of this House the "surplus test" should be restored so that no exports of natural gas from Canada would be permitted unless it could be shown that volumes slated for export were surplus to Canadian needs reasonably projected over the 25 year period following the commencement of the proposed export.
What is so magic about the figure of 25 years? Why not a figure of 35 years or 15 years? The legal text which sets out the mandate and responsibilities of the National Energy Board in the area of licensing of natural gas exports does not refer to a magic number. Let me quote in part from section 118 of the National Energy Board Act which sets out the considerations applicable to the issuing of licenses:
On an application for a licence, the Board shall have regard to all considerations that appear to it to be relevant and, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, the Board shall
(a) satisfy itself that the quantity of-gas-to be exported does not exceed the surplus remaining after due allowance has been made for the reasonable foreseeable requirements for use in Canada having regard, in the case of an application to export-gas, to the trends in the discovery of-gas in Canada; -
There are three things to note about section 118. It provides a mandatory responsibility using the word "shall". It is within the sole purview of the NEB and it gives no indication or direction as to responsibility. There are no magic numbers or formulas in that text, and it provides no one way of doing things. Indeed, the National Energy Board has seen fit to modify its surplus determination procedures.
June 16, 1989

Let me review the various hoops which the surplus test, so dear to the Hon. Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Harvey), has gone through since 1959. Generally speaking, the model first established by the Alberta Energy Resources Conservation Board, the National Energy Board has used a formula approach to determine volumes of gas that are surplus to reasonably foreseeable domestic requirements. The methodology has been adapted according to changes or perceived changes in market conditions; that is, the methodology has tended to be more exacting when gas markets are tight and energy prices are rising, and more flexible when markets are soft, prices falling and supplies shut-in.
In the 1960s, a decade of resource discovery, development, and market expansion marked by little or no concern for supply and pricing, the National Energy Board used a stock approach. From established reserves, that is recoverable reserves, the Board deducted total requirements, that is a lump sum for Canadian sales, usually 25 per cent of the actual or forecast demand, plus a lump sum for authorized exports. The balance, if any, was considered to be available for exports. This formula approach did not take into account the increase or decline in demand, nor in future reserve additions, thus it was always possible to overestimate or underestimate a variable.
In the 1970s, energy markets changed very abruptly. Low prices had increased the North American gas demand, but also discouraged resource developments. At the same time, oil price shocks had fuelled worldwide concerns about energy security. The National Energy Board switched its attention from the adequacy of reserve bases to the adequacy of deliverability, that is the industry's ability to produce gas over a given period of time. In 1979, the Board added to its reserves test to deliverability tests, one based on the level of deliveries, and the other based on established reserves. All three tests had to be satisfied before exports could be authorized.
In the early 1980s, the gas market again changed dramatically. There was restrained demand, mature infrastructure, underutilized capacities, and surpluses were now the major characteristics. Thus, in 1982 the National Energy Board made some changes to surplus procedures, adopting a more realistic assessment of total
Natural Gas Exports
requirements, that is, what actually would be sold versus what was licensed or contracted for sale.
In 1985, while negotiations leading to natural price deregulations were under way, and that is the time that this is taking place, the National Energy Board decided to review surplus procedures to determine their appropriateness in the light of anticipated policy and market changes.
In the spring of 1986, the Board introduced a surplus methodology based on the reserves/production ratio. The object was to maintain a ratio between reserves and production.
In September, 1987 the board announced that its current reserves to production ratio would no longer be appropriate, and it would be contrary to the free market operation if the level of gas supply to Canadians were to be determined by other than market forces. The Board moved to a market base procedure which is comprised of two elements, one of which is a public hearing component to air complaints and assess the impact of the proposed export and to determine whether the national public interest is being met as stipulated in Section 118 of the Act.
May I remind my hon. friend from Edmonton East that this new market base procedure was announced more than one year before the passage of the Free Trade Agreement? Thus, one cannot accuse the National Energy Board of bowing to the pressures of the Free Trade Agreement.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   ENERGY NATURAL GAS EXPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me today to speak on the motion presented by the Hon. Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Harvey).

June 16, 1989
Natural Gas Exports
Mr. Speaker, the natural gas surplus test established by the National Energy Board was based on the principle that the best way to ensure our energy security was to keep large amounts in reserve. This was an interventionist approach that substituted a bureaucrat's reasoning for the laws of the market. The Government believes that the best way to guarantee a secure natural gas supply is to ensure that markets work correctly, not to distort the rules.
It is said that those who do not learn from history are condemned to repeat the same mistakes. The energy crises of the 1970s were an excellent lesson. The main lesson that these upheavals in the petroleum market taught us is undoubtedly that any excessive government intervention is likely to do more harm than good. The history of natural gas is proof.
In the early 1970s, the surplus test was a large obstacle to the gas trade between Canada and the United States. According to this test, the National Energy Board would only approve exports if, in its opinion, Canada had sufficient reserves to meet its own needs for 25 years.
Mr. Speaker, the application of this test had three negative effects. First, we lost major export earnings, since the Board did not authorize any new gas sales outside of Canada between 1970 and 1979. Second, one form of intervention leads to another. Since the door was closed to exports, there was so little competition on the domestic market that the Government was obliged to regulate the domestic price of natural gas. Third, the natural gas producers were encouraged to develop gas that no one needed so that it could be put in reserve and included in the calculation for the surplus test.
It is extremely difficult to calculate what this policy has cost Canadians as a result of inefficient operations and in terms of foregone income. It probably amounts to billions of dollars, Mr. Speaker. Furthermore, Canada's reputation as a reliable trading partner has been tarnished.
Did Canada enhance its security of energy supply by creating such reserves? Not at all, Mr. Speaker. In fact, the surplus test points to a basic lack of understanding of the laws of the energy market.
In the case of oil, there is the constant threat of a sudden disruption of world supplies. More than half of the world's oil reserves are located in the Middle East, a
region that suffers from political instability. Furthermore, most of the oil in Eastern Canada is imported. That is why the Government has introduced policies to deal with any disruption of supply. More specifically, the Energy Supplies Allocation Board would be able to activate a number of allocation and rationing programs should an emergency situation be declared. Canada is also a member of the International Energy Agency, whose emergency sharing system would guarantee that no member country would suffer unduly in case of a worldwide disruption of the oil market. Thanks to measures of this kind, Canadian oil consumers are protected against any interruption of supply, without adversely affecting the efficient operation of the oil market in our country.
In the case of natural gas, we do not have the same problem. Canada produces practically all the gas it uses, so that occurrences on the market outside North America do not really have an impact on our own market. In fact, we have no reason to expect a sudden disruption of the gas market.
Our major concern is therefore not that our access to natural gas might suddenly be cut off but that someday we might exhaust our supplies, so that consumers would be out in the cold, so to speak. Are we right to worry? Not at all, Mr. Speaker. If governments let the markets operate the way they should, none of this will happen.
In the early 1970s, some people predicted that we would have a shortage of natural gas before the eighties. In fact, in 1979 we had a surplus. What happened, Mr. Speaker? Despite government intervention, the market did its work. Prices rose, which caused production capacity to increase and consumption to slow down. When the same thing happened in the United States, there was a drop in demand for our exports. That is why the expected shortages never materialized. In fact, as governments changed their perspective and encouraged the substitution of gas for oil, the anticipated shortage changed into a glut.
Does that mean that we must always go from one extreme to another, from shortage to surplus? Not if we are prepared to accept the laws of the market as more efficient than rules made by bureaucrats in determining the ideal rate of depletion and in choosing the best forms of alternative energy or fuel saving! However, we do not need the "surplus test" to make sure that Canadians never run out of gas. If we let market forces operate,

prices will always adjust so that supply and demand remain in balance.
What about the long term? After all, is natural gas not an exhaustible resource? Mr. Speaker, as the price of natural gas rises, consumers will adopt other energy sources. Nothing leads us to think that this change will be rapid or disruptive. We already changed from one form of energy to another in the past, with no great economic consequences.
In the 1870s, 90 per cent of Canada's energy came from wood. In 1920, it was only 16 per cent, while coal accounted for 75 per cent. Fifty-five years later, in 1975, coal's share had fallen to 10 per cent, while oil accounted for 54 per cent and gas for 22 per cent. Everything suggests that the future transition from oil and gas to nuclear fusion and hydrogen or any other form of fuel will be just as easy. Furthermore, coal consumers started to use oil or gas long before coal ran out and we can expect that natural gas consumers will go to some other source of energy long before gas runs out.
All this does not mean, Mr. Speaker, that the Government has no role to play in the natural gas markets. Obviously, market forces can fail. The present market-based procedure serves to ensure that Canadians have fair access on normal business terms to their own natural gas supplies.
Mr. Speaker, I would be negligent if, in closing, I did not talk briefly about natural gas from an environmental point of view. Gas is the least polluting of all fossil fuels because it produces less sulphur dioxide and carbon dioxide emissions than coal or oil. Sulphur dioxide contributes to acid precipitation, while carbon dioxide adds to the greenhouse effect. Building up gas reserves therefore does nothing to safeguard the environment. On the contrary! If Canada exports less gas, the United States will probably bum more oil and coal. We should encourage the use of natural gas, not limit it!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to speak on Private Member's Motion No. 97 of the Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Natural Gas Exports
Harvey). It gives me pleasure to endorse the deregulate-denvironment of Canada-U.S. natural gas trade.
Recent regulatory and policy initiatives have created a framework that allows the industry access to market opportunities. That also provides a method of oversight to ensure that exports are in the over-all public interest.
Allow me to review the accomplishments of the natural gas industry. Canada has the most competitive natural gas market in the world. Our competitive market is working to the benefit of both producers and consumers. With the achievements to date, our industry is in an excellent position to withstand and benefit from the energy market volatility that seems to lie ahead. In short, we have a success story in which we can take pride.
It is worth noting that our natural gas deregulation policies were primarily driven by developments in and the objectives for the Canadian gas market. After all, 60 per cent of the marketable gas produced in Canada is consumed at home. Tangible evidence of the success of deregulation is the increased competitiveness and market responsiveness of the Canadian natural gas prices. The weighted average domestic price for the years 1987-88 is more than $1 per gigajoule lower than the pre-deregulated price of $2.79 at the Alberta border. In turn, this has increased the competitiveness of gas vis-a-vis alternate fuels and enhanced the ability of industrial gas users to compete internationally. A similar degree of progress has been achieved in the natural gas export industry. Volume wise, 1988 was a banner year for natural gas exports. Exports of 1.27 trillion cubic feet in 1988 surpassed the previous record established in 1972 by roughly 25 per cent. As a result of these export sales, Canadians captured roughly a 7 per cent share of the total U.S. natural gas market, the largest portion ever.
On a regional basis, imports of Canadian gas assume a greater importance. For example, about 30 per cent of total California supply comes from Canada and about 71 per cent in the Pacific northwest. Certain border accommodation markets such as Vermont and upstate New York are entirely dependent on Canadian gas.
Although the surge in export volumes has been accomplished by a decline in average export prices, gas export revenues grew 15 per cent in 1987 to reach $3 billion in

June 16, 1989
Natural Gas Exports
1988. In Canadian currency, this represents the first major increase in revenues in three years.
Notably, Canada-U.S. trade in natural gas has not been one way. One of the offshoots of Canadian gas deregulation has been the reactivation of U.S. exports into our eastern markets. To date, the volumes have been small, less than 20 billion cubic feet, and limited by capacity constraints, although still strategically important both from a price discovery point of view and ensuring greater flexibility and security in gas supply systems.
It is perhaps worth remembering why Canada-U.S. trade in natural gas began at the turn of the century and subsequently prospered. For the U.S., Canadian gas offered the proximate long-term supply security needed for market development. In several instances, U.S. markets were closer to Canadian supply than to lower 45 production.
For Canada, exports provided the economies of scale needed to finance the major pipeline systems which attached supply to market, and were also a means of generating producer cash flow.
Although we have a surplus of natural gas relative to domestic demand, Canadians have always been somewhat ambivalent about exports. Recognizing both the importance of natural gas in meeting our total energy demand of 30 per cent and the non-renewable nature of the resource, Canadians have consistently sought reassurances that exports would be in the public interest. This ambivalence has been reflected, virtually since the turn of the century, in policies and consequent legislation and regulations governing pricing and licensing of natural gas exports.
However, historically, regulatory policies on both sides of the border have tended to distort prices and limit levels of gas demanded. Both the Canadian and U.S. Governments have worked hard over the past five years to place bilateral gas trade on a competitive, market-oriented basis.
In Canada, the regulation of gas exports is carried out by a federal agency, the National Energy Board, and includes three major functions. They are to ensure that gas to be exported is surplus to reasonably foreseeable domestic requirements; to establish tolls and tariffs, that is, conditions of access, for Canadian pipelines serving domestic and export markets; and to issue certificates of
public convenience and necessity for the construction of interprovincial and international pipelines.
We have been particularly fortunate in that our governing legislation and the regulators who implement it have been sufficiently flexible to adapt rapidly to changing policy and market circumstances.
A case in point, consistent with domestic deregulation, the NEB replaced a rigid formulaic approach in place for 25 years, with a market-based procedure to determine if gas to be exported is surplus to Canadian requirements. The procedure has three components. They are the ongoing monitoring of and reporting on specific market gas developments and over-all Canadian energy supply market trends. This is intended as an early warning system to alert industry to possible future market disruptions.
The second component is the public hearings at which applications for long-term-in excess of two years-export licences are reviewed to determine over-all public interest.
The third component is a complaints procedure to ensure that no Canadian user is unable to contract for supply under terms and conditions similar to those in a proposed export arrangement.
To date, the new procedure has been used successfully to assess several export licence applications.
The Free Trade Agreement with the U.S. is a logical extension of this earlier deregulation process. The Free Trade Agreement basically entrenches the conditions under which exporters are able to compete actively in U.S. markets and gain market share. However, a form of public review and export-import licensing does remain in place for the following reasons: to obtain statistics on trade; to ensure orderly marketing; to monitor supply and demand trends; to ensure broad public interest criteria are met; and to ensure that there is no discrimination in the access to markets or to supplies.
Given these initiatives, what is the outlook for Canadian gas exports? Clearly, long-term exports for general system supply will continue to be the backbone of our natural gas trade. However, thanks to the flexibility of our export policy, Canadians have become active players in the U.S. spot market. Some 25 per cent of the volumes flowing are under short-term orders. Indeed, the willingness of Canadian producers to sign long-term export contracts provides them a competitive advantage in the U.S. market vis-a-vis their American counterparts. U.S. producers have demonstrated a reluctance to submit to
June 16, 1989

similar terms and their contracts frequently relate to "well deliverability".
Canada has significant proven and potential gas supplies in both the western sedimentary basin and in frontier regions. For example, at year-end 1986 Canada had roughly a 25-year supply available from remaining reserves of 72 trillion cubic feet. With frontier discoveries included, the established reserves are estimated at 89 trillion cubic feet. Thus we are well placed to take advantage of new market opportunities.
However, at present levels exports are reaching the limits of capacity. Additional volumes to meet growing U.S. demand will require the construction or expansion of systems in Canada and the U.S.
Mr. Speaker, it has been a great honour for me to take part in this debate.

Mr. Speaker, first, let me apologize to you for my rather husky voice. Let me say that while we are talking on the subject of hydrocarbons I could use some form of hydrocarbon for my voice.
I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Harvey) for having been able to introduce a Private Member's Motion into the House at such an early date in his career. It surprised me a bit that somebody from Alberta would want to put a clamp on the export or use of hydrocarbons from Alberta. I would have expected someone like myself from Ontario to be one who might fall for the idea of trying to limit the use of natural gas.
This is a motion with which I perhaps would have agreed some 15 or 25 years ago. However, I think the passage of time has suggested that perhaps this thought is outdated. Indeed, the National Energy Board surplus tests for natural gas was based on the belief that hoarding our energy supplies was the best way to ensure energy self-sufficiency or security. That policy is definitely an interventionist policy. It has as its objective to substitute bureaucratic wisdom for natural market forces. I think that is where the problem lies. I know that my hon. friend from the NDP perhaps would not like to
Natural Gas Exports
talk about the natural market forces. However, history shows that they do work.
It is a belief of the Government that the best way to ensure that security of natural gas supplies is not to override market forces but to make the markets work. It has been said that those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it. There is much to learn from the two energy crises of the 1970s. Unquestionably, the prime lesson to be derived from the ups and downs in the petroleum sector is that excessive government intervention can do a lot more harm than good. Indeed, the history of the natural gas surplus test is a case in point. By the early 1970s, the surplus test represented a major constraint on the trade of natural gas from Canada to the U.S. In accordance with this test, new exports of natural gas were permitted only if, in the view of the National Energy Board, sufficient gas reserves existed to satisfy Canadian needs for 25 years. This test had three major negative effects. First, there was a significant loss of export revenues between 1970 and 1979, which of course had a big effect on Alberta producers. There were no new exports of natural gas allowed.
Second, intervention begat intervention. With the export markets cut off, there was virtually no competition left in the Canadian market. The Government then had to regulate the domestic price of gas.
Third, natural gas producers were given an incentive to develop gas that nobody wanted so that it could then be shut in and included in the surplus test calculation. It is extremely difficult to estimate the cost to Canadians of this policy in terms of the inefficiencies that were created and the revenues that were lost, but it would likely be in the billions of dollars. In addition, there was the damage to Canada's reputation as a reliable trading partner.
Did Canada enhance its security of supply by hoarding its gas supplies in this fashion? No, because the surplus test represents a fundamental misunderstanding of how energy markets work.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that I am running of time, but I would be remiss if I did not add a word about natural gas and the environment. Natural gas is the cleanest burning of the major fossil fuels. It produces fewer sulphur dioxide emissions than oil and coal and fewer carbon dioxide emissions. Sulphur dioxide contributes to acid rain and carbon dioxide contributes to the greenhouse effect. Hoarding of natural gas therefore will not help the environment. In fact, the opposite is likely to be true.

June 16, 1989
Natural Gas Exports
If Canada exports less natural gas, the U.S. is likely to bum more oil and more coal. We should be encouraging the use of natural gas, not prohibiting it.
